t: And You, the Horseman Who Cries “Patience!”
x: And you, the horseman who cries “Patience!” … when speech and neighing alike have died away And you, the horseman who cries “Patience!” … when speech and neighing alike have died away “He says: you are the one who steadies the army in patience, telling them: patience, patience under the bite of war, when the ordeal has grown immense and the fighting fierce, so that a man can no longer speak, nor a horse neigh” (al-Wahidi) In reverses, when hardships descend, silence takes over and people hold more and more inside. You see them putting off the moment they burst into laughter or tears until the battle is over.. Everyone puts off victory, Except the master, the leader: he speaks good tidings and calls for patience in the eye of the storm, in the thick of the dust! He does not leave it until the end; right away, now, he says: Rejoice, good is coming. And that is no easy task, He is staking everything! He is defying! Wagering on victory, against the harshest odds. Ah, Abu al-Tayyib! Your words have reminded me of the sayings of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that history has made immortal, as he steadied the believers in the midst of battle: The Battle of Uhud: { [Remember] when you [fled and] climbed [the mountain] without looking aside at anyone while the Messenger was calling you from behind. So Allah repaid you with distress upon distress so you would not grieve for that which had escaped you [of victory and spoils of war] or [for] that which had befallen you [of injury and death]. And Allah is [fully] Acquainted with what you do }[Surah Al Imran: 153] Remember when you were turning your backs and fleeing across the land, (without looking aside: not turning to look at anyone) Notice! Look closely! They do not turn to look at anyone: they have fallen silent, holding everything in. Some are consumed with working out how to save themselves, for the army has broken, defeat has begun to seep through the ranks, and the scattering and dispersal have begun. And the Messenger ﷺ, the master, the leader, did not lose his patience or his composure. He called to them from behind their backs (calling you from behind): “To me, servants of Allah! To me, servants of Allah!” And at Hunayn, when some of the believers turned and fled, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called out among them: “I am the Prophet, and there is no lie about it; I am the son of ʿAbdul Muttalib.” So the leader, in times of crisis, brings people good tidings of relief and of good, steadies them in patience and holds patient alongside them, and does not leave it until the end.

t: The Let Them Theory
x: Leave them to do what they do: the blocking, the rebuffing, the scheming, the shutting out — all by the will of Allah! And none can lift it but Him! Leave them to do what they do: the blocking, the rebuffing, the scheming, the shutting out — all by the will of Allah! And none can lift it but Him! Because every attempt to correct them, change them, convince them, win them over, falls under "the desire to control" — and the only thing you can ever control is yourself. That is why there is nothing to be gained from fretting over them! { And thus We have made for every prophet an enemy — devils from mankind and jinn, inspiring to one another decorative speech in delusion. But if your Lord had willed, they would not have done it, so leave them and that which they invent } [Surat al-An'am: 112] Had your Lord willed, they would have been on your side, and dear to you! But He willed, in His wisdom, that they be your enemies. So can you change a thing Allah has written for you? No. So the best way to handle it: leave them to lie! Let them scheme! And let them mock you. Leave them! Because letting go is not leaving your life in chaos; it is freeing yourself to put your own life in order, instead of being consumed by that terrible, overwhelming chaos the hotheads leave in their wake — a chaos you can never, however hard you try, tidy, make sense of, or set right again! "Letting go" does not simply mean letting things run their course; it is a conscious choice to free yourself from this primal urge to control" (Mel Robbins, p. 55) So letting go does not mean you are weak. That comes from the illusion of being in control {You are not over them a controller } [Surat al-Ghashiyah: 22] Because feeling weak and helpless is a negative feeling about something you cannot fix or handle; what it really means is that you leave others as they are! (Mel Robbins) Leave them! They are the ones who chose loss, and they are the ones who chose to go astray. So leave them; let the hopes they live in keep them distracted, and let their numbered days dress up what they are in, until they see it as everything, the greatest thing of all! Leave them! You are not answerable for them, and you will not be called to account for them. Leave them, for they will be repaid for their evil deeds in this world before the Hereafter; it is only a matter of time, so be patient and let them be. { Let them eat and enjoy themselves and be diverted by [false] hope, for they are going to know } [Surat al-Hijr: 3] Leave them to delight in their little; ahead of them lies much to keep them busy.. All they are in is a slow drawing-on toward ruin, but their sensors are switched off, so they take it for blessing and breakthrough, for provision and victory. Leave them in their arrogance, swelling until it becomes tyranny, until they rebel, and come to misery. (But the people divided their religion among them into sects — each faction, in what it has, rejoicing (53) So leave them in their confusion for a time (54) Do they think that what We extend to them of wealth and children (55) Is [because] We hasten for them good things? Rather, they do not perceive (56). (Al-Mu'minun) Leave them to think their tyranny is judgment, and their ignorance knowledge (their confusion, ghamratihim : their misguidance and their ignorance). I left them to themselves — but until when?! Until the Day of Resurrection! { So leave them to converse vainly and amuse themselves until they meet their Day which they are promised } [Surat az-Zukhruf: 83] So turn away from them entirely, and busy yourself with the worship of your Lord, with your work, your learning, your life; they are not worth the waste of your time, your thoughts, or your feelings. Your deferred revenge: And what is a deferred victory but a deferred revenge on those who set themselves against you?! { So leave them until they meet their Day in which they will be struck insensible } [Surat at-Tur: 45] { And whoever is patient and forgives — indeed, that is of the matters [requiring] determination } [Surat ash-Shura: 43] Forgiveness makes sense here, since the verses speak of the wronged taking back their right — but why patience? Because pardon takes a great deal of patience: swallowing your anger, reining your impulses back, even while you have it in your power to take revenge and press on toward justice! Letting go is a choice and a decision, because you have the very same power, the very same choice, to punish! They are two options, equally within your power and reach (pardon = justice) "Someone once said to me: it's as if you are "allowing it," without actually allowing it." (Mel Robbins) Think how many times you have plotted punishment: I'll do this, I swear, and I'll say that. Then, you do, nothing. How much time have you burned thinking, and how many nerves have you frayed! And in the end you choose to let it go, because you know it is the wisest course, the most mature, the most complete, the surest shield against childish slips like flaring up in anger — which hardly suit someone as grown-up as you ! Tell me: when was the last time you lost your temper, frayed every nerve, and it actually worked?! Rarely, very rarely. Do you remember the Facebook message you fired off, boiling over with rage? And the voice note where you went through the roof? Tell me, honestly, by God: didn't you regret it, even a little! Admit it — admitting feels good, and it helps us make conscious decisions, and better ones in the future. For the grudge before you let go, and the anger after it, are of no use at all: a waste of time, and a squandering of the standing you hold.

t: (And What Is That in Your Right Hand, O Moses?)
x: (And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?) He asks, though He, Glorified and Exalted is He, knows it better than Moses himself — yet He asks in order to put him at ease! The Lord, the Exalted, wanted Moses, peace be upon him, to feel at home in the conversation before surprising him with the weighty mission (Go to Pharaoh. Indeed, he has transgressed)! Imagine if He had opened the conversation with that command! Moses would have sensed apprehension within himself and felt estranged! But He wished to set him at ease first, so He asked him about the staff — a staff He knew, and could see in his right hand. (And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?) He asks, though He, Glorified and Exalted is He, knows it better than Moses himself — yet He asks in order to put him at ease! The Lord, the Exalted, wanted Moses, peace be upon him, to feel at home in the conversation before surprising him with the weighty mission (Go to Pharaoh. Indeed, he has transgressed)! Imagine if He had opened the conversation with that command! Moses would have sensed apprehension within himself and felt estranged! But He wished to set him at ease first, so He asked him about the staff — a staff He knew, and could see in his right hand. It's like saying to a child: Ooh! What's this toy in your hand? And you know perfectly well what it is! You can see it — but you want to put him at ease and be gentle with him, or to prepare him for being asked to play with his brother. Now imagine you had said to him first: Give me the ball! ( hāti , with a kasra, is said to a boy and a girl alike.) He would have bristled, shied away from you, and run off. (And what is that in your right hand, O Moses? (17) He said, "It is my staff; I lean upon it, and I bring down leaves for my sheep and I have therein other uses." (18) [Allah] said, "Throw it down, O Moses." (19) So he threw it down, and thereupon it was a snake, moving swiftly. (20) [Allah] said, "Seize it and fear not; We will return it to its former condition. (21) And draw in your hand to your side; it will come out white without disease — another sign, (22) that We may show you [some] of Our greater signs." (23). Moses, peace be upon him, felt at ease, and so he began listing the staff's uses, when he could have stopped at: It is my staff. But so deeply at ease was he with Allah that he went on to count off its other uses, which means the question had achieved its aim — the knower's feigned ignorance: (And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?). Then He commanded him to throw down the staff, and when it turned into a snake he was afraid of it; so his Lord reassured him: just as He has the power to turn it from a staff into a snake, He has the power to turn it from a snake back into a staff. So after ease came fear, and then his soul was soothed and felt safe. Then He gave him still more strength, confidence and firmness, commanding him to draw his hand in beneath his other arm, and it would come out white — a sign more reassuring still, and stronger proof that his Lord was with him and had complete power. A reading of the inner state of Moses, peace be upon him: so far he has felt ease, then fear, then safety, then strength and ever greater firmness And what came next? His Lord charged him with the heaviest mission and the hardest command, and all those exchanges had been nothing but a preparation of heart and mind for accepting it: (Go to Pharaoh. Indeed, he has transgressed) Notice that Moses, peace be upon him, never once objected. It is something strange and wondrous, and to this day it astonishes me! Let's imagine a different scenario: The moment Moses came before his Lord, He commanded him at once: Go to Pharaoh! The reaction might well have been: Why?! But Pharaoh is a tyrant, and, and, and… But He had prepared him for this command beforehand, in many ways: putting him at ease, and letting him witness the power of Allah the Exalted (That We may show you [some] of Our greater signs) — so that you may believe, so that your soul may settle, grow calm and be at peace; just as it found peace in His commands and in His power to turn the staff into a snake and then back into a staff, so that you may know that I am able to do all things, that I am Strong — and this means that I am with you! Moses, peace be upon him, felt that peace, and so he accepted the hard command the instant it was laid upon him, meeting it with no objection — not even a question about the details: How? Who? When? And from the depth of his heart's tranquillity and his soul's contentment with the command of Allah the Exalted, he turned to Him in prayer: (Go to Pharaoh. Indeed, he has transgressed. (24) [Moses] said, "My Lord, expand for me my breast [with assurance] (25) and ease for me my task (26) and untie the knot from my tongue (27) that they may understand my speech. (28) And appoint for me a minister from my family — (29) Aaron, my brother. (30) Increase through him my strength (31) and let him share my task (32) that we may exalt You much (33) and remember You much. (34) Indeed, You are of us ever Seeing." (35) [Allah] said, "You have been granted your request, O Moses." (36). From this we come to see that language is a social art, not mere words and musical rhythm. So if you want to be socially intelligent, be linguistically intelligent first. Language teaches you social tact and good manners: gentleness, preparing the listener's heart before a direct command or prohibition, taking things step by step, and knowing how to engage with others. If someone were to build thousands of relationships yet lacked care and precision in choosing his words, those relationships would fall apart, and he would fail with people and with his own family. Language is the root of social life. I recommend al-Maydani's al-Balāghah al-ʿArabiyyah ; it is good on this subject.

t: What Deserves Tears and What Does Not: Reflections on the Weeping of the Prophet ﷺ
x: 1- The forbidding of tears over what lies ahead: what Ibn al-Qayyim called “the weeping of fear” (Zad al-Ma’ad). 1- The forbidding of tears over what lies ahead: what Ibn al-Qayyim called “the weeping of fear” (Zad al-Ma’ad). Weeping over something you fear may happen in the future comes from Satan, and such weeping does not become a believer. Let him seek refuge in Allah from Satan, the accursed. For this belongs to the unseen: what do you know of whether the thing you dread will happen or not? And suppose it does happen, what do you know of the gentleness and mercy Allah will show you! And if what you fear does come, it will be something you are given the strength to bear. Look back at your past, at the things you dreaded that did come to pass: did you not marvel at Allah's gentleness and mercy toward you! And here you are today, alive and provided for, among us, laughing! So why weep over what lies ahead? It is nothing but time thrown away. This fear-mongering is Satan's work (That is only Satan who frightens [you] of his supporters) “When the Prophet ﷺ sent him to Yemen, he (peace be upon him) went out with him, Mu’adh riding and the Messenger of Allah walking beside his mount. He said: ‘O Mu’adh, it may be that you will not meet me after this year of mine, and that you will pass by my grave and my mosque.’ And Mu’adh wept, stricken at parting from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He said: ‘Do not weep, O Mu’adh, for weeping is from Satan.’” (Sahih, with a break in its chain) He forbade him only because it concerned something yet to come. So hold back your tears from whatever lies ahead of you, and come: on this journey of ours, let us learn what they are worth shedding for. 2- Weeping over what is lost of this world “She said: By the One in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, I could tell the weeping of Abu Bakr from the weeping of Umar while I was in my room. And they were, as He said, merciful among themselves. He said: So I said: Then what did the Messenger of Allah do? She said: His eye would not shed tears over anyone; but when he was grieved, he would simply take hold of his beard” I do not know the chain of this report, but it has come in another wording whose narrators are trustworthy, though some of them are disputed: I said to Aisha: Did the Messenger of Allah ﷺ weep? She said: No, but he would grip his beard ﷺ. Reflect on the hadith: a- He wept over no one, because his heart was wholly bound to Allah, because he wanted nothing of this world, and because he had given himself to the Hereafter as a yearning lover gives himself to the one he longs for. Whatever is lost of this world is not worth a tear. b- Restraint, then redirection: first he masters his tears and holds himself back, so that they do not fall but stay held in his eyes; then he turns this bodily expression away from tears and into gripping his beard or chin. This means he had reached the summit of mastery over his emotions. And do not be surprised that a righteous person can reach such a level: whoever has let go of his cravings, found his solace in the Quran, and stripped himself of this world will find this restraint easy When a young man is used to wading into death, the easiest thing he crosses is the mire; and he who commands the fortresses, and they never defy him, the rugged highlands and the plains obey. (Al-Mutanabbi) c- Weeping over someone is mercy: it is established that he ﷺ wept over his son Ibrahim (peace be upon him), and this weeping was born of mercy and tenderness, as Ibn al-Qayyim says in Zad al-Ma’ad. So behind the believer's sorrow there is an awareness that steers it: he weeps out of mercy, not out of regret for what is gone; his tears are the tears of one who seeks his reward with Allah, not the tears of resentment. And how far apart the two outlooks are. 3- Weeping over the past I divide it into two kinds: 1- Weeping over the distant past: weeping over something that years have passed over. This is not to be encouraged. It is not established that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, years after the death of Khadijah or of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), used to weep! Rather, he grieved for them, felt tenderness and longing for them, and remained loyal to the dead. It is in the very way the human mind works to look back on the distant past as beautiful, with all its sweetness and all its bitterness. Do you weep over your childhood? No, you call it the good old days. This is what is known as rosy retrospection: we let the bad of the past fade and remember what was good and lovely. And the further the past recedes, the more time goes by, the stronger this bias becomes. This very hour you see in a rather negative light; but once it is a day old, then a week, its shadows fade and it turns rosy. The optimist leans toward remembering the blessings of the past, and clears his mind to recall how lovely a past it was; the pessimist leans toward remembering its darkness, its afflictions rather than its blessings. This does not mean we must never look at the past in a negative light; we need to, but without drama! Without tears, without brooding, standing apart from the feelings of that time, and looking fairly at the lessons we took from it. That is why the soundest course is that, as the years go by, a person comes to accept Allah's decree, makes peace with the distant past, and gives himself to his present. 2- Weeping over the recent past: something close to your present, within the span of months and weeks. There is no harm in this. 4- Weeping out of anguish, resentment and regret: anguish at Allah's decrees and refusal to accept them, or regret over the fleeting portions of this world. All of this ought to be given up. How he ﷺ wept: Not with noise and wailing, but quietly, with tears that welled and ran down without sobbing; and when his weeping grew strong, they would hear a sound from his chest like the simmering of a pot. Finally, these ideas can be lived; they are not ideals out of reach. Begin with what is easiest and put it into practice. Each time, practise one more thing. For example, begin with what is easiest for you: not weeping over the future. Then the next easiest: not weeping over what years have passed over (the distant past). Then the hardest: not weeping over this world and what you have lost of it (the recent past). That said, there is nothing wrong with weeping! We are not talking about obligations! These are only reflections; but when you put them into practice, try them out and test them, you will be amazed at how your inner wellbeing has grown happier and steadier than before. And changing this behaviour is simply a decision you make; it can be changed “From Aisha, who said: We were returning from Hajj or Umrah and were met at Dhul-Hulayfah. The young men of the Ansar were coming out to meet their families. They met Usayd ibn al-Hudayr and gave him the news of his wife's death, and he covered his head and began to weep. I said: May Allah forgive you! You are the companion of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, with all your precedence and standing, and you weep over a woman? She said: He uncovered his head and said: You are right. By my life, I have every reason to weep over no one after Sa’d ibn Mu’adh, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said of him what he said. She said: I said: And what did the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say of him? He said: The Throne shook at the death of Sa’d ibn Mu’adh” (its chain is hasan) See how Usayd ibn al-Hudayr was weeping over his wife, and then resolved to weep over no one after Sa’d ibn Mu’adh, may Allah be pleased with them both And experience and the years play their part. This, and Allah knows best; and success comes only from Allah.

t: Is Artificial Intelligence Eroding Our Social Intelligence?
x: Communication is the easiest skill of all — or so you think? Yet the interview published in Harvard Business Review, titled: How AI Is Changing Communication: Weighing Efficiency with Efficacy. Communication is the easiest skill of all — or so you think? Yet the interview published in Harvard Business Review, titled: How AI Is Changing Communication: Weighing Efficiency with Efficacy. shows us that communication is critical thinking. You read your manager's face before you speak to him, and then you make the right call: is today a good day to bring it up? You also use creativity to weave your words together, and after every conversation your memory replays the details: if it was delightful, you laugh to yourself! And if it was flat, or went badly, you ask yourself: where did it go wrong? Did I slip up? Did I come across well? How do I feel about her — at ease, indifferent, put off? Do I keep up this relationship or let it go? How does she communicate? What are her tactics when she talks? And all the other questions of appraisal, which mean that we think, remember, analyze, and make decisions based on what is in front of us. Your communication skills, as they stand today, are the sum total of everything you have lived through: the fruit of your culture, your personal growth, the lovely smiles, the hard experiences, and the embarrassing moments. And when we lean on AI entirely to communicate with others, what we are really doing is handing the responsibility over to it: "My co-founder, Brian, has this line, 'You can delegate the work, but you can't delegate the accountability.' And so if I'm not reviewing the output, if I'm not paying attention to the quality of the work, that reflects back on me… At the end of the day, the most important thing is the quality of your communications." You used to run into social problems and then think your way to a solution, and so, over time, you learned to master your emotions and to handle mistakes; you built a distinctive social system of your own, and reached a brilliant level of social intelligence. And when we use AI to excess — letting it answer clients' messages, pick the right jokes, and socialize on our behalf while we look on from the sidelines — we undermine our social skills, or, to put it most truthfully: we erode the social intelligence we toiled to develop, labored to refine, and built up through experience after experience of making and creating, until we became the shape and the singular selves we are today. AI may push you to overdo emotional expression, even though the real you is a person of few words. And with these stiff, mechanical replies, it wears away your real capacity to feel for others. Those machines raise walls between us and the other person — someone who, had we only spoken to him, might have revealed remarkable gifts, or a mind gone to waste! For it is human conversation that lays bare both the flaws and the potential. Spontaneity and quick wit are the height of social intelligence: to answer with confidence and speed, without preparation, without notes to read from. You feel triumphant when you fire back a dazzling retort at your opponent, and you boast about it and tell the story to others; or you regret your words, and you learn. AI may wipe out spontaneity, shatter that dazzling quickness of wit, and swap it for ready-made answers, frozen like ice cream. The threat to who we really are in society AI may erase who we truly are. Whether your manner is firm, or you are witty and full of fun, AI replaces it all with a manner that is forever positive, scrubbed of any negative feeling and of all harshness and sternness — unlike human nature, whose moods shift with the place and the hour. AI must not take away your unique voice and your distinctive way of arguing. AI flatters endlessly and trades in positive feelings, and it is almost dim-witted when it comes to grasping negative feelings and the words a heart keeps hidden — that hidden reading only an intelligent human can pick up. When we let AI reply in our place, we erase the truth of who we are in that moment: short sentences mean we are irritated right now, or that we are sending the other person a message — one he understands between the lines — that we would, please, like to end the conversation. That machine, on the other hand, never stops its pompous chatter: would you like me to summarize all of the above in a statistical table? So that I can know how you really speak — the real you, expansive and lavish with words, or the cheerful, daring one, or the one of clipped phrases and a crowded schedule — you have to show up! Show yourself to us in the truth of your mood and your moment, just as you are right now! Stop hiding behind that cold machine and its sweet, friendly words. Tell us who you really are, tell us about your mood right now, about your hard day, about the joy in you that has room for hours of talk! The trouble with AI is that it does not let you understand what the other person says as it truly is — and look at yourself when you use it: it does not always understand you. No chief executive can hear the real voice of his employees through this machine. Wade Foster was asked about his experience developing a "Wade bot," and he said: I have a whole host of models I use to build a bot that imitates me, but even so it only gets 80, 90% of the way there. My experience tells me AI is strong at coding and weak at communication. My co-founder said: it sounds cold and does not respond to the text, not like a human voice, which reveals the truth of the self through the text. And on the bright side, we can train AI to imitate the way we talk, so that it becomes our partner in producing the podcast. Social learning AI will not give you the free experiences and hard-won wisdom of others, the kind whose lessons you learn so that they spare you disasters that could cost you thousands of riyals — those inspiring conversations you take as messages meant for you, after which you change for the better; no machine can take their place: do you remember a conversation with someone that changed you for the better? We learn even from our enemies, and we cannot learn from this endlessly flattering machine the way we learn from them! The danger AI holds over us stalks the beginner who uses it to excess; and as for the expert, it may wreck all he has learned, or make him forget some of it. "People are getting more nervous the more they're using AI because they realize that the output is pixel perfect, but it's not really their synthesized information. If you think about it, communication is the end result of a whole long process. Communication is operationalized critical thinking, and if we outsource that critical thinking and then are put on the spot to answer questions, to give input, to give an update, people get really anxious because they realize they don't have that depth of knowledge and the critical thinking behind it. And so it is really important not just to review the output, but to really review the thinking so that when you're put on the spot, when you have to respond, you have that confidence that you know what you're really thinking and speaking about." "Again, it kind of just depends on the task. AI is this fantastic tool and to not use it I think would be a mistake. It could be a lot better if you use it responsibly… there is this sort of comprehension gap that's kicking in when you don't use AI responsibly, where you're sort of delegating almost too much. And as you get asked questions about this thing, as you start to investigate, you realize, 'Oh, I don't actually know enough about this area that I should.' But there could be areas where the impact is relatively low and you're fine delegating the work to the AI more fully. And so it just comes down to the judgment here."

t: My Lord, Make Me Forget What Has Passed, and Help Me with What Remains
x: When Qaylah (may Allah be pleased with her) lost her son, she wept before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and told him of all the responsibilities his death had left on her shoulders: When Qaylah (may Allah be pleased with her) lost her son, she wept before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and told him of all the responsibilities his death had left on her shoulders: “So I wept, then said: By Allah, O Messenger of Allah, I bore him a resolute man, and he fought alongside you on the day of al-Rabadhah, then he went off to bring me provisions from Khaybar, and its fever struck him, and he left the women in my care” So he counseled her to supplicate, saying: “My Lord, make me forget what has passed, and help me with what remains” (a hasan hadith) Here we learn that a person may ask Allah to make him forget the past and what he lost in it, and to help him through what is left of his life. And we learn that the best way to deal with a past that is gone is to forget it; and if he cannot forget, let him ask Allah to make him forget, and turn to the present and tend to it, and ask his Lord to help him carry the burdens and duties he has taken on — never imagining that help comes from anyone but Allah. “By the One in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, were you not a poor woman, we would have dragged you on your face today” — or “you would have been dragged on your face” (Abdullah was unsure) — “Is one of you unable to keep kindly company with his little companion in this world, and then, when one more entitled to him than he comes between them, to say: ‘Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return’?” For Allah has more right than you to the one you lost.

t: Don't Tie Your Fate to Your Faith
x: I have a piece of advice, precious and essential: don't tie what is decreed for you to your faith, or its strings will start to tremble. I have a piece of advice, precious and essential: don't tie what is decreed for you to your faith, or its strings will start to tremble. Don't say, "This came to me because of that good deed," or you will become one who reminds Allah of his favors; nor, "That came because of a sin," or you will despair. Then your faith will sway to the right and to the left: rising when circumstances are kind, crumbling when the decree is hard. When you worship Allah, worship Him for His sake alone. Don't tie small decrees and passing events to this great meaning of faith, or you will stumble about like a night-blind camel; your soul will be shaken, your strength blunted, and your sun will set. Say: I do not worship You for hardship, nor for ease; I worship You only for the sake of Your Noble Face, seeking Your pleasure and Your Gardens. And stand firm on this. Then see the deep inner calm you will rest in. Note: This does not deny that hard decrees may be what a servant has earned by his own hands, nor that he should call himself to account and look over his life, so that he repents and changes for the better. The point here is that faith should settle in his heart and take root there, so that he is neither insolent in times of ease nor despairing in hardship.

t: The Delight of the Art of Listening to the Noble Quran
c: Branches of the Relationship with the Quran
x: Dr. Saeed Hamza, an expert in Quran memorization, says in his book and courses "The Five Fortresses" that alongside your daily portion of reading, you need a daily portion of listening to the Noble Quran: no less than 30 minutes a day, roughly 41 verses, or say four to five pages, half a juz', a hizb. Dr. Saeed Hamza, an expert in Quran memorization, says in his book and courses "The Five Fortresses" that alongside your daily portion of reading, you need a daily portion of listening to the Noble Quran: no less than 30 minutes a day, roughly 41 verses, or say four to five pages, half a juz', a hizb. Perhaps he drew it from the hadith: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to me: (Recite Surat an-Nisa' to me). So I recited until I reached {So how [will it be] when We bring from every nation a witness and we bring you, [O Muhammad] against these [people] as a witness?} [An-Nisa: 41]. He said: Then either he nudged me, or I turned, and there were his eyes, flowing with tears ﷺ" And know, may Allah keep you, that nothing touches the soul and stirs the heart and the feelings like listening. Nothing at all. You cannot imagine what wonders it works: renewing your presence of heart, softening you into humility, sharpening your reflection. How many a written reflection was born from listening! The soul tires of any single method, such as reading alone, and grows restless with it. And don't say: I'm busy! I can barely, barely get through my reading portion, and now you want me to listen as well! No, that's too much. We can find time for anything, if we truly want it (And if they had intended to go forth, they would have prepared for it [some] preparation). So how do we make it happen? 1- Make it a daily habit; build it into your plan and your daily routine. 2- Start with just a few minutes, then let it grow over time (even a 10-second clip; yes, I'm serious) 3- Speed up the recording! -we'll come to the condition later-. 4- Listen during routine tasks, such as driving. Don't listen to recordings of the Quran from prayers! Why not? Because the imam is human, and prone to slips and lapses: he may swap one verse for another, or forget it altogether. So listen to the Quran only from recorded, recited mushafs that have been checked and reviewed, such as the King Fahd Mushaf, or from apps such as the Wahy app. See the King Fahd Complex apps here: qurancomplex.gov.sa/apps/ Don't say: but some YouTube channels cut out the mistakes and fix them. Don't say that. I once listened to a complete mushaf put out by the Affairs of the Imams and Muezzins of the Grand Mosque in Makkah, and it had 3-4 mistakes the editors had missed -again, mistakes are only natural; the imams are human like us, and my only aim is to alert anyone who cares about listening to the Quran- sometimes the imam slips and brings the Warsh reading into Hafs! And someone who knows nothing of the qira'at may memorize that pronunciation, take it for the Hafs reading, and recite it and repeat it! He may even think it is a refinement of tajweed, a mark of masterful precision! The poor soul has no idea he has made a mistake! Check: if you suspect the imam has made a mistake, look it up in the mushaf and correct the verse right away! That way you won't pick up the wrong reading -and how many times this habit has saved me!-. I still remember memorizing some verses from a Taraweeh prayer, recited by one imam in a sweet voice, and then discovering, months later, that there was a mistake in what I had memorized. I wondered where the mistake had come from, and found it was the very clip I had been listening to and memorizing from: he slipped, so I slipped, and I memorized the slip! And the mistake took root in my memory! Just imagine the trouble of correcting it: to this day I am still struggling with it, and sometimes I slip again, and I say: if only I had heeded the advice from the start: listen only to recorded mushafs. The pull of prayer recordings is their soaring spirituality, boundless and endless, and a beauty of voice you will never find in a recorded mushaf. Listen to them -there's no harm in it- I do so myself at times, but I always find mistakes -I said always, not rarely or sometimes, that is, when listening to a whole surah of medium or long length, apart from a few, and those from the most renowned for precision-.! But train your ear on the precise, recorded mushaf. Should I speed up the recording? Yes. I have read that speeding up Quran recordings is permissible, on condition that the letters and words do not run into one another, or blur into a babble from which nothing can be understood. Don't you use hadr , rapid recitation, when you read? Well, this is hadr for listening. All right, but there's a problem! Go on! Sometimes my mind wanders, I get drowsy, and I have no idea what the reciter is saying? Pay no mind to the whisperings of Satan, and keep listening even if you didn't focus, reflect, or understand. Let's leave perfectionism aside! And listen to what Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: He said: I heard Abdullah ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal say: I heard my father say: I saw the Lord of Might, the Mighty and Majestic, in a dream, and I said: O Lord, what is the best thing by which those who seek nearness to You draw near? He said: My speech, O Ahmad. He said: I said: O Lord, with understanding or without understanding? He said: With understanding and without understanding. (Manaqib al-Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ibn al-Jawzi) Among the courtesies of listening to the Quran: after listening to poems, chants, and the like, the righteous predecessors would close with a recitation of the Quran, and some of them would recite both before and after; perhaps the wisdom in this is to clear away heedlessness, revive the heart, and bring it back to faith. (See al-Ghazali's Ihya' 'Ulum al-Din , the chapter on Listening) Should my listening portion be different from my reading portion? Whatever suits you! It is better for your listening portion to differ from your reading portion, so that if you stop at a certain minute, you pick up from there the next day. And keep your reading portion separate, so that you have two completions running: one by reading and one by listening. And if you would rather have the one complete the other, there is room for that too! There is a wonderful idea -though hard to put into practice- which is to listen while reading some tafsir at the same time. For that I recommend the Wahy app (31 encyclopedias of tafsir, working offline and free of ads. Look up how to download the books and the audio) Don't set yourself ideal, perfect conditions, for they are exactly what keeps you putting off listening to the Quran: insisting, for instance, on listening only to the mujawwad mushaf, or only to a certain reciter whose tajweed is hard to follow, or only with full focus and attention, or only slowly at 1x speed. Every one of these has stood between you and finishing your listening portion. So start now, without these conditions. Put it into practice this very hour; don't say tomorrow, because you will forget, and a deed that follows on the heels of a moving word is the one that lasts! For those who memorize: one tried-and-tested way of correcting your recitation is to listen and move your lips along without speaking aloud. The aim is to catch your own mistakes in memorization, recitation, and tajweed. If you recite aloud with the reciter, you may not hear him clearly, and you may not notice your own mistake, because your voice drowns out his. I have found this to be the best way yet, after a teacher, to catch mistakes in recitation and correct them. If this has benefited you, then remember the writer of these words in your good prayers.

t: The Greatest Danger of Fame
x: In a podcast episode, the guest, a chef, recalls that as his fame grew, he began to want a homely, family feel in the frame, after years of standing alone in the lens, In a podcast episode, the guest, a chef, recalls that as his fame grew, he began to want a homely, family feel in the frame, after years of standing alone in the lens, First he showed his wife, then his children, then little by little the wider family, the grandmother too, Then he voices his bitter, aching regret: if only I had never brought my family into the picture, The podcaster: Why? The family burst apart. The grandmother and the mother fell out, and the feud runs on to this day; his wife divorced him; the siblings who used to gather together scattered. I used to think people looked at you with the same innocence you looked at them with. But there are people who watch you laughing with your family, teasing your wife, playing with your children, while they themselves have none of this, and envy creeps in. At the start of the road, the star shines alone; then he wants more and brings his family in. And once he reaches that point, he has reached the greatest danger of fame: losing the most sacred of all social circles, the family. I went to this celebrity's channel to look for his latest videos. These days he appears only with strangers and other guests, never with his family. It seems he has learned his lesson. But the question remains: have we learned it?

t: Magnifying Bad Outcomes
x: It is in the very nature of human perception to magnify the negative outcomes of the bad experiences that befall us. It is in the very nature of human perception to magnify the negative outcomes of the bad experiences that befall us. And that is one enormous psychological trap! If you knew that this very cast of mind lay behind the collapse of giant companies, you would never again take lightly this nature you already know so well. Okay?! So what's new? I know that out of dozens of compliments, we remember the one criticism we heard. I know.. thanks, I learned nothing 😳 Okay, bear with me! Now, you can't change this nature. - Understood! But there are tactics you can put to work, and force yourself into, to break this perceptual habit: magnifying bad outcomes. - What are they? First- Just be aware of it: understand it, and notice it when it comes. That's all; don't do anything else. That alone is a huge step forward. - Okay, next! Second- Start a happiness file! Digital or paper, whichever you like, and gather into it the best news, the kindest comments, and the brightest moments of your life! And whenever your brain, true to its nature, starts blowing up the negatives, make yourself, drag yourself if you have to, even when you don't feel like it, open that file and read something in it! You'll find your sharp bad mood has broken, or let's say the blowing-up of negatives has dropped from 100% to 70–60% What's happened is that you've broken that edge, that ugly magnification, and so afterward you'll make decisions more rationally; you won't rush in, blind and unthinking, and make hard-line decisions on the strength of a sharp, soaring bad mood. Always be on the lookout for some pleasant, positive technique that takes the edge off (an outing or a stroll, a chat with an old friend, jokes and banter with a colleague at work,, anything that lifts your mood) and make yourself do it even if you don't want to, and say: My dear self, I want what's good for you! You must look at this file, so that you don't make reckless decisions and hurt people who've done nothing wrong, all because of an ugly, soaring, razor-sharp magnification in your perception! - Aha! Really useful So glad 😌 And don't forget to like, share, and subscribe to the channel 😂

t: What Is the Bright Side of Artificial Intelligence?
x: The lesson was so hard that even its teacher told us it was not easy to learn. The lesson was so hard that even its teacher told us it was not easy to learn. Artificial intelligence taught it to me in 10 minutes, and I understood it with ease, through example after example. I doubted what AI could really do, and feared it was only flattening my mind! So I went to a recorded academic lecture on the subject, given by (an actual human being)! The very same examples the AI had given me — he used them! And when I say the same, I mean exactly the same! And I realized I had spent 40 minutes of my life on a human lecture to get what AI gave me in 10. AI is just like a teacher: a good teacher explains things to you with perfect clarity, is sincere with you, and makes the material simple, because he wants you to surpass him; and surely you have met the bad teacher too, the one who tangles the material, stretches the explanation far beyond what it needs, and leaves it all in fog. So take AI as an expert coach and teacher in whatever fields you want to grow in! ☀️

t: Similarity and Difference
x: Similarity wraps us in a sense of familiarity, though in the clever it stirs a faint suspicion; difference, on the other hand, rings far more true. Similarity wraps us in a sense of familiarity, though in the clever it stirs a faint suspicion; difference, on the other hand, rings far more true. What I mean is this: the disturbed person is the one who tries to match you in everything. You went through such-and-such? So did I. You live in such-and-such a country? Me too. You love coffee juice? Just like me. I don't deny that real similarities exist. My point is that, with time, the disturbed person's contradictions come to light: you find out he doesn't read at all, isn't from that country, and has failed the vocabulary test (coffee juice). And that is why clever people grow wary of similarities. Difference, though, rings truer. When you disagree with someone, there may be arguments and quarrels between you, even a brief chill, and yet you feel you are talking to a real human being. We admire the way someone reacts differently from us, and the more we admire, the more we follow their example. We imitate those who differ from us; in those who resemble us we find nothing to imitate, let alone to admire.

t: What Do You Lose When You Let AI Do Your Understanding and Learning?
x: You lose your mind's power to analyze, to decode, to understand, and to solve problems You lose your mind's power to analyze, to decode, to understand, and to solve problems Instead of wrestling with a knotty sentence, straining to picture it and grasp it, you run to AI. Yes, it hands you the understanding, quickly and precisely You feel like a quick learner, sharp and perceptive But the price you paid was your own ability to imagine, to analyze, to understand, And as you know, a child who leans too much on his parents grows up weak in character and in mind. So what of a grown adult who leans on algorithms for everything? He is pampered, yes, but his inner life is frail and his mind has gone slack. I am all for AI: for using it, experimenting with it, building on it. But draw lines around it and ration your use. Not everything is for asking it, or it will steal your mind away. And not everything is for demanding of it. Isn't that what life itself has taught us: that it never gives us everything?

t: The Place of Artificial Intelligence in the Quran
x: ([Dhul-Qarnayn] said, “This is a mercy from my Lord”) ([Dhul-Qarnayn] said, “This is a mercy from my Lord”) Sheikh Muhammad ibn Ali al-Shinqiti says: Dhul-Qarnayn counted the building of the barrier a mercy, and so buildings, airports, and the internet are all a mercy as well. He said this in his tafsir of Surat al-Baqarah, bringing in this verse from al-Kahf along the way. And when I reflected on how the Quran and the Sunnah treat tools and machines, I found that they never condemn the thing itself; they condemn its use, when that use is bad. Surat an-Nahl is example enough: it counts out blessing after blessing, among them horses, mules, clothing, armor, and more; and elsewhere in the Quran there are ships, means of travel, iron, the firmly anchored cauldrons, and on and on. Yet the Quran and the Sunnah censure those who misuse them: through extravagance, or by beating animals, treating them harshly, and showing them no gentleness. Artificial intelligence, likewise, is a blessing and a mercy, and let us not forget that the critique belongs to how it is used, not to the thing itself. And yes, it has its harms, just as it has its benefits! But for some to wage war on artificial intelligence altogether and write it off entirely, that is the greatest mistake of all!

t: On Campaigns to Boost Followers
x: To those who message me privately (with campaigns to boost followers and likes) To those who message me privately (with campaigns to boost followers and likes) - There is a scholarly consensus, as far as I know, that trading in followers, buying them or selling them, is forbidden; for in doing so you deceive your followers: people take them for real followers when they are a phantom audience. (So seek out another source of income, lawful and wholesome; I am truly a sincere adviser to you) - And then, my dear ones: by Allah, I spent three years studying fame and wrote a study on it (Fame and Celebrities: A Study of the System, Forms, Process, and Possible Theory); I read sixty English books on public relations, the very field that makes stars and celebrities, and wrote a book on it; my bachelor's degree is in public relations, and I studied marketing for three months… None of this is to show off! It is to tell you, my son, my daughter: I have the skill and the knowledge in this field (fame), but not the desire! I do not want a phantom audience. A person, I believe, once fully mature, cannot fool himself by letting his soul live on rosy illusions of fame, manufactured stardom, and counterfeit praise, only to find, when he reaches for the reality, nothing but ashes. And I cannot bear even half a second, or a quarter of one, of living in psychological, mental, and social self-deception. This is a sickness! This is madness! A pestilent breeding ground of cursed, lying deception. - Finally, we all have the natural longing for a crowd and a little shine. But every time my own soul wants to take the crooked paths here and there to win fame and spread its name, I remind it of the permissible ways, for they are the best, the purest, and the most God-fearing: making content and organizing it; “natural” marketing, public relations, press, and advertising campaigns that grow a real audience steadily and unhurriedly, with nothing wrong in them; and walking slowly, step by step, instead of the sudden, rapid growth that throws mental and social functioning into disarray and does more harm than good. - And even so, for all that I do, there are those who impugn my intentions and my direction -and I keep silent and do not trade word for word- for some have said to me: you fame-seeker, you who are empty of meaning! Some hint at showing off! And some send me long, sprawling sermons on sincerity in private, and I know exactly what they are driving at; yet I meet it all by ignoring, pardoning, and letting it go. And I say to myself: this, too, is a trial! I know that some of my dear ones do not agree with me in this approach, and may see in it a harshness toward oneself; but the path has become clear to me in this matter. For every dilemma, Allah has given us a clear and healing guidance that leads us along the plainest road and the soundest way, and, most important of all, the middle one.

t: The Complex Number
x: The complex number a+bi is made of two parts: The complex number a+bi is made of two parts: The real part (a), and the imaginary part with its coefficient, bi A complex number needs its complex conjugate, the same number with the opposite sign, and all of this so that it can shed its imaginary part and keep only the real: a-bi And then this breathtaking thought struck me ✨ We too, in life, need a companion who runs counter to us, intellectually, culturally, and in what we know, to help us strip away and erase the imagined, illusory parts of ourselves The more complex numbers you meet, the more conjugates whose sign is the opposite of yours, the wider your view of life grows, and the more moments of wonder you reach! Your brain gets rewired, you take quite a few knocks to the head, and your way of researching and your way of thinking are transformed. Conversations across different cultures, too, have a great power to change the way you think. But if you stay within the same social circle (the same field, the same philosophies, the same age, the same interests..), all you are doing is adding more copies of yourself! So how, I wonder, will you ever grow and change?!

t: Why Do People Restore Their Accounts After Deleting Them?
x: The research question is no longer why people delete their social media accounts, but why they try to get them back 100 days after deleting them ? The research question is no longer why people delete their social media accounts, but why they try to get them back 100 days after deleting them ? The account-deletion revolution was sparked by Lanier's latest book, "Ten Arguments for Deleting Your Social Media Accounts Right Now," which quickly shot to the top of bestseller lists around the world. The book came out in 2018, and from there the delete-Facebook campaigns ran on into 2019. What the researchers found was hilarious! Because the people who deleted Facebook simply moved over to Instagram 🌚. (It's like boycotting Starbucks coffee and having a croissant for breakfast;)) Media studies also found that most of these serial deleters and restorers are young Gen Z-ers and millennials; the explanation is that they grew up with the iPad and all things digital, and find it hard to let go. Older people, aged 50–65, are different: when they delete, they rarely come back. Driven by nostalgia, and a deep spiritual longing for those platforms. In one experiment, researchers paid $100 to anyone who would deactivate Facebook. The result was astonishing: 95% went back and restored it 100 days after deleting it. — Some studies say users regret deleting their account after 30 days, the very window social apps give you to recover it, 32 days; and I propose extending it to three menstrual periods, like the ruling for a divorced woman ;)) During the Facebook crisis, the question people searched for most on Google was: How do I delete my Facebook account? And after 2019, once the crisis and the massive deletion campaigns had died down, the top questions on Google became: How do I get my account back? How do I report my deleted Facebook account? One social researcher argues that these platforms have come to make up a large share of our identity; they have become part of how we define our very selves, and they are hard to leave. Yes, life is not what it used to be. And now I see people who oppose artificial intelligence attacking it ferociously, and I've noticed that most of them are over 40 or 50! So I made my peace with them, and forgave them, for exactly that reason: go easy on them, they're getting on in years. Thank God, the young aren't swayed by their critical opinions and their fierce rejection And the world of research moves on, with you or without you, and fast, thanks to these technologies; humanity has never seen a generation learn as quickly as this generation of young people, So you want us, just to please Your Highness, to slow down in our research and learning because you have philosophical issues with artificial intelligence!? And I came across someone criticizing a piece of research done with artificial intelligence, Come here, you critic: what have you ever contributed?! And criticizing the professional designer who uses it Come here, you: what have you ever designed?!! Unbelievable!

t: Identity
x: Identity gives us steadiness and stability, shelter and safety; yet in the very same measure, it keeps us from seeing the truth Identity gives us steadiness and stability, shelter and safety; yet in the very same measure, it keeps us from seeing the truth It drives us to defend the selves we used to be, and pulls us into blind fanaticism and a mind shut tight. t: The Story of William James Sidis
x: Now then, friends, let's talk! Now then, friends, let's talk! Come, sit over here! Let me tell you a story, and then tell you something that matters to you. If you'd rather skip the story, that's fine; but what you miss, you miss! William James Sidis (1898-1944) was the most astonishing of prodigies, with an IQ estimated at somewhere between 250 and 300. He was reading the New York Times at eighteen months, and at two he taught himself Latin, with no help from his parents, at three he learned Greek, at four he learned to type in English and French, and at five he wrote a paper on anatomy, at eight he finished high school, he very nearly entered Harvard as a small child, but Harvard decided not to admit him until he had matured socially; he finally went in at eleven, at sixteen he became a professor with honors, he predicted black holes ahead of the astronomers of his day, and the boy had barely come of age before he could speak forty languages! And then what became of this boy of dazzling feats and towering gifts? He withdrew from society entirely. He could not bear being hounded by the press, and he suffered nervous breakdowns. I think you see what I am driving at with this story, young man!? Yes, exactly! You may have a brilliant mind and pile up one achievement after another; but if you do not work at building the inner skills, the psychological, the social, and the spiritual, in your relationship with Allah, then with yourself and with others, your intelligence can crumble at any moment, and quick success can turn into a source of pain and failure. For these skills are what give you the wisdom to live your life, and what keep your success and your intelligence intact; without them, success is always one moment away from collapse. I want you to know this too, early in life, before it is too late: gaining wisdom while you are young matters more than specializing, more than scholarly achievement or professional success! Live your life with wisdom (by seeking out the art of deepening your bond with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and by building your psychological and social skills). As for narrow specialization and mastery of the sciences: yes, they matter, but do not make them sacred! Wisdom always comes first, and if you hurry to reach it while you are still young, that is a great achievement an achievement no one sees, an inner one, yes, but it is the ground you stand on. If you manage to live with wisdom and true success, then by all means, enjoy every success that follows! I forgot to tell you how the story ends! William left the university at twenty and walked away from every intellectual pursuit and pastime, and in 1924 a journalist found him working in a humble office on (Wall Street) for meager pay. When the journalist questioned him, he answered that he no longer wanted to do any work that weighed on him. And so he stayed, in a lowly, ordinary job, cut off from science and mathematics, until death came for him at forty, after a brain hemorrhage.

t: “They say, ‘Perish not of grief; be steadfast’”| Reflections on the Command Not to Kill Oneself with Grief
x: The Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful opens Surah Ash-Shu'ara in the most dazzling way: The Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful opens Surah Ash-Shu'ara in the most dazzling way: (Ta, Seen, Meem (1) These are the verses of the clear Book (2) Perhaps, [O Muhammad], you would kill yourself with grief that they will not be believers (3) He makes clear that the disbelievers drew no benefit from the Book, so do not be like them, killing yourself with sorrow because they will not believe; even grief brings no benefit. Just as they gained nothing from the shining truth, you gain nothing by killing yourself with sorrow. Bākhiʿ means one who kills. It comes from bakhaʿa : to carry the slaughter all the way to the bikhāʿ , a vein at the nape of the neck. That is the furthest point a slaughter can reach, and when it is reached, the soul departs. (al-Tafsir al-Muharrar) And Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: (And do not kill yourselves [or one another]. Indeed, Allah is to you ever Merciful (29) (An-Nisa) Perhaps one way of killing the self is to crush it under gloom and grief until it can no longer step back into the joy of life, or return to the things that once made it glad. So if He has forbidden you to kill it with grief, then you must rouse it with every permissible delight until gladness and joy come back to it! There are only two roads. Either you kill yourself with grief, weighed down by sorrow over life's worries and over people, or you bring yourself joy, giving back to your soul its lost right to delight and its missing share of everything sweet and gladdening. And since we are still in Surah Ash-Shu'ara, The Poets , the poets have matchless gems on this very meaning, such as the one who chanted: O you whose soul is being slain by longing for a thing the Fates have taken from his hands He calls out to him with the vaguest of addresses: O you there, killing yourself with grief over something the Fates naḥathu , turned away, from him. (Then perhaps you would kill yourself through grief over them [ ʿalā āthārihim ], [O Muhammad], if they do not believe in this message, [and] out of sorrow) (Al-Kahf) What is asked of you is this: do what you were commanded, fulfil your duties, and take the means as you strive toward your goals. Then if the ends prove out of reach, if your efforts fall short of them and the Fates turn them away, there is no call to burden yourself with grieving over them “In this verse and those like it there is a lesson: the one charged with calling people to Allah must convey the message and strive by every means that leads to guidance, and close off the paths of misguidance and error, to the utmost of his ability, relying on Allah in all of it. If they are guided, well and good; if not, let him neither grieve nor sorrow, for that weakens the soul and wrecks one's strength, and there is no benefit in it. Rather, he should carry on with the task he was charged with and set out to do; whatever lies beyond that is outside his power” (al-Tafsir al-Muharrar) The point is this: there is no sense in a grief so heavy that it kills you, buries your thoughts and your creativity alive, and ends your life over what has passed and is gone. To destroy yourself with excessive gloom, to deny yourself life's joys and pleasures for the sake of this sorrow, has no meaning and no use, except to breed more of the same sorrow! Sorrow begets sorrow, round and round in a circle that never ends. So forcing yourself to be patient is better for you than forcing yourself to grieve! Pressing your soul toward the joy of life and leading it to its pleasures, even when it is unwilling, is better than leaving it in a sorrow that brings nothing you wish for and settles nothing you seek. Going forward in joy, busying yourself with a worthwhile hobby or useful knowledge, with work, with talk among people, unfurls sails of happiness that carry the ships along, and perhaps they will bring you to an island you never imagined. For joy strengthens the soul and the will, so it grows strong enough to work, moves with zeal and energy, and the sails of opportunity open before it And sorrow, what does it do?! It produces: nothing. Helplessness and sloth. It is the killing of life and the slaughter of the soul. Dead land is brought back to life by human hands; and your own soul, you are the one responsible for bringing it to life, and you, too, are the one who slaughters it with crushing grief. And Imru' al-Qais says: Halting their mounts over me there, my companions ... say: “Perish not of grief; bear it with grace” And I picture it as though Jibril, peace be upon him, had stood over his head, consoling him, urging him not to kill his soul with worry (Then perhaps you would kill yourself..) “He says: they halted over me, that is, for my sake, or standing over my head while I sat beside their camels and mounts, saying to me: Do not perish from excess of grief and depth of anguish; adorn yourself with patience. In short: they halted their mounts over him, bidding him be patient and forbidding him to give way to anguish.” (Sharh al-Zawzani) And look at the word he chose: tajammal ! It holds bearing up, and it also holds making yourself beautiful, reaching for everything that gladdens the soul and lets joy in. He must push himself to it even if he does not want to open his shut-up soul, even if it can see nothing but its own closed doors. And people say in everyday speech: “ Tajammal , there's nothing left!” They say it when the effort is spent, the mind has been driven to exhaustion, and fatigue and weariness have climbed over the walls. They say it to cheer you on: You've reached your goal! You're right there, so why turn back now? Can't you hold yourself together for the last step? Do anything at all, just get there! Put on a brave face, be patient, endure, anything! Just get it done! The English have something like it, a lovely expression; they say: “Burn the midnight oil” That is: when your work is nearly finished, stay up with it late into the night and see it through to the end, whatever it costs you in sleep and fatigue. And our own fellow says: “Lift the curtain of night and undo its braid, and take no rest but on the tops of the high peaks” Tarafa ibn al-Abd says: Halting their mounts over me there, my companions ... say: “Perish not of grief; be steadfast” “ Tajallud : making oneself hardy, that is, holding oneself to patience.” (al-Zawzani) It seems the poets say (perish not) at the parting of loved ones. The Quran is different. It says ( bākhiʿ ), and it opens with a word of reasoning; it shields the soul of the Prophet ﷺ from being made common, so it does not aim the perishing at his very self as the poets do (perish not of grief). Instead it guards his noble soul ﷺ, choosing the language of reasoning (perhaps you) over a direct prohibition. And it uses bākhiʿ , an active participle, naming the one to whom the act of bakhʿ , killing oneself with grief, belongs. It uses the active participle to bring the good news swiftly and to dispel the illusion! Yes, because crushing sorrow is born of illusion, not reality. The extra sorrow in it does not match the facts or what actually happened. Such grief carries an exaggerated, overblown reading of events; it is an extremist reading of what happened! So let us fight extremism in thought and in feeling! As for bringing good news swiftly, it is like saying: Blessing has come! The companion has come! Here the active participle ( bākhiʿ ) is brought forward to forbid the soul and steer it away from harmful sorrow, to lay bare what that sorrow really is, and to strip away the deceit of Iblis, who saddens the believer's heart with what is not real, what brings no benefit and is in fact deeply harmful, unless Allah permits (Private conversation is only from Satan that he may grieve those who have believed, but he will not harm them at all except by permission of Allah. And upon Allah let the believers rely (10) (Al-Mujadila) Iblis: the name comes from iblās , utter despair, for he despaired of Allah's mercy forever. And we have been forbidden (and You know best) to resemble him or follow him. So keep yourself far from crushing worry, for it is Iblis's first step toward other steps. And know that Satan has many roads to saddening the believers, because bringing grief into the believer's heart is a goal in itself for him: it saps the believer's strength for worship and his drive to do good. To reach that goal, he will use any means Nor is it limited to two people whispering together. Al-Mawardi said, explaining what is meant by private conversation from Satan: “it is the dreams a person sees in his sleep.” “And whoever brings grief upon the believers bears a likeness to Satan” (al-Tafsir al-Muharrar) So the believer takes the Quran as his model in being good news for the believers: he brings gladness into the hearts of believers and spreads hope, while whoever resembles Satan spreads gloom and brings grief into people's hearts. “He, Glorified is He, likened this to a man whose loved ones and dear ones have parted from him, so that he is falling apart with regret over their traces, killing himself with longing for them and yearning at their parting. He brought this singular image to guard His comparison from being made common; for Allah the Exalted wished to console His Prophet ﷺ and to lighten the worry and pain that had come upon him, so He presented the situation in the form of hopeful expectation, then perhaps you , though what is meant is prohibition, that is: do not kill yourself, do not destroy yourself, out of sorrow that they do not believe” (al-Tafsir al-Muharrar) Because killing yourself with deep sorrow weakens the soul, and a weakened soul is of no use: it neither worships Allah gladly and with contentment, but only grudgingly and in pain, nor does it benefit itself or others! “Al-Kisa'i said: bakhaʿtu al-arḍ by farming, when you have made the land weak by plowing it over and over; and a man bakhaʿa himself when he wore himself down. On this basis, the meaning of ﴿ bākhiʿun nafsaka ﴾ is: wearing it down and straining it until you destroy it” al-Razi. For crushing grief (may the Most Kind, the Most Merciful watch over you) weakens your soul even for worship, dampens your resolve, and stands between you and the earning of good deeds and higher ranks. Over their traces: Āthār , traces, belong to the past; and these two poets stood over the ruins of the past, weeping. And people commonly speak of someone who died ʿalā athar , on the traces, of a loved one! That is: when the first one died, his traces and signs remained, his clothes, his perfume, and the other stood grieving over those traces for a while, until he followed him into death and perished too! “It is said: so-and-so died ʿalā athar so-and-so, meaning after him. The origin of this is that when a person dies, his signs and traces remain for a while after his death, then they fade and vanish entirely. So if his death comes close upon the death of the first, it happens while the traces of the first still remain, and so it is right to say: so-and-so died ʿalā athar so-and-so.” (al-Razi) The Quran urges you to leave a trace, instead of weeping over one! For in the first lies your life, and in the second your death. Have you not heard what the Lord of Might has said?! (Indeed, it is We who bring the dead to life and record what they have put forth and what they left behind [ āthārahum ], and all things We have enumerated in a clear register (12) (Ya-Sin) Their traces: We record what they did and the practices, good or bad, that they set going in their lives and that people followed after them; so it is either a reward for them or a burden upon them. So always set this choice before yourself (may the Most Merciful watch over you) whenever a deadly grief confronts you: 1- Either I waste my time weeping over a dead trace (of no use whatsoever) 2- Or I make the most of my life by building up the earth and filling it with what benefits me and others, and I leave good traces after my death that flow back to me as rivers of reward and the richest of good deeds, and they bring me joy. So choose for yourself. You are free now. I commend you to Allah.

t: The Days Will Show You What You Did Not Know
x: The Prophet ﷺ loved this line of poetry and would often repeat it; it is by Tarafa ibn al-Abd: The Prophet ﷺ loved this line of poetry and would often repeat it; it is by Tarafa ibn al-Abd: The days will show you what you never knew, and news will reach you from one you never fed for the road. The days will lay bare, and events will bring to light, the things you did not know, and the news will be carried to you by a man you never asked for it, and to whom you gave neither provisions nor wage. (al-Zawzani, The Concise Commentary ) And news will reach you from one for whom you never bought a traveler’s pack, nor set for him a day to keep. The news will be brought to you by one for whom you never bought goods for the journey ( batātan ), and for whom you never fixed a set time or appointment to bring it; rather, the truths appear to you of their own accord. (Same source) His lovely lines brought to my mind the words of Allah the Exalted: (For every happening is a finality; and you are going to know) For every happening is a finality : a truth that will come to pass, even if after a while — Ibn Kathir That is, every report Allah the Exalted gives has a time or a place in which it comes to pass, without fail and without delay. And if you take al-mustaqarr to mean ‘settling,’ the meaning is that every promise and every threat from Allah the Exalted must settle into reality, and they will surely know, when it appears and descends upon them, that the matter is just as Allah the Exalted said. As for that with which He warned the disbelievers, it may mean the punishment of the Hereafter, and it may mean the Muslims’ prevailing over the disbelievers in this world through war, slaying, and subjugation. al-Razi Every report in the Quran has a reality … and it covers both the threat of the Hereafter and the threat of this world, and each has its finality. And from al-Suddi: what He had been promising them of punishment came to pass on the day of Badr. And and you are going to know is joined to the sentence ﴿For every happening is a finality﴾, meaning: you will come to know it; that is, it is unknown now, and you will know it in the future, when it descends upon you. And this fits most clearly with the threat of punishment in this world. Ibn Ashur

t: Breaking Divorce with Rays of Radiance
x: The end of the surah is a prelude to its beginning! The end of the surah is a prelude to its beginning! (It is Allah who has created seven heavens and of the earth, the like of them. [His] command descends among them so you may know that Allah is over all things competent and that Allah has encompassed all things in knowledge (12) (At-Talaq) Why did Allah create the heavens and the earth? His command descends among them! And what is that command? It is the one set out at the surah's beginning! (O Prophet, when you [Muslims] divorce women, divorce them for [the commencement of] their waiting period and keep count of the waiting period, and fear Allah, your Lord. Do not turn them out of their [husbands'] houses, nor should they [themselves] leave [during that period] unless they are committing a clear immorality. And those are the limits [set by] Allah. And whoever transgresses the limits of Allah has certainly wronged himself. You know not; perhaps Allah will bring about after that a [different] matter (1) (At-Talaq) Perhaps Allah will bring about after that a [different] matter: a good decree that lay beyond your knowing You know not — perhaps Allah will decree things you cannot foresee. And you see Him say it a second time: His decrees reach beyond your present knowledge of how things stand, for His knowledge spans the past, passes beyond the present, and knows the future (And when they have [nearly] fulfilled their term, either retain them according to acceptable terms or part with them according to acceptable terms. And bring to witness two just men from among you and establish the testimony for [the acceptance of] Allah. That is instructed to whoever should believe in Allah and the Last day. And whoever fears Allah - He will make for him a way out (2) And will provide for him from where he does not expect. And whoever relies upon Allah - then He is sufficient for him. Indeed, Allah will accomplish His purpose. Allah has already set for everything a [decreed] extent (3) He provides for him, decrees for him, and brings about for him a matter he neither knows nor foresees, for human knowledge of the unseen falls short. Once again: why did Allah create the heavens and the earth? Between them descend affairs and decrees, provisions and arrangements. Yes — why?! When you see His power in creating them, you come to know who this God is who arranges your affairs and decrees them (so you may know that Allah is over all things competent and that Allah has encompassed all things in knowledge) He has set for everything a [decreed] extent — because He is over all things competent! Everything has a limit where it ends! Illness has its measure, and its limit is healing; misguidance has a limit, and He decrees guidance after it; poverty has a measure where it stops and turns into wealth; ignorance has its measure, and it is knowledge. And so every hardship, however great, has a measure where it ends. So go easy on yourself, quiet your fear, and set your mind at rest. And know that Allah's knowledge encompasses the days, past and future, time and place; He knows everything about them, And you — what is your knowledge beside His? (You know not - he does not expect). You cannot reckon, imagine, or foresee His decrees and His knowledge, however far you reach and however hard you try, So isn't it better for you to lay down your limited knowledge and entrust it to His limitless knowledge? Yes — and far more restful! (And those who no longer expect menstruation among your women - if you doubt, then their period is three months, and [also for] those who have not menstruated. And for those who are pregnant, their term is until they give birth. And whoever fears Allah - He will make for him of his matter ease (4) That is the command of Allah, which He has sent down to you; and whoever fears Allah - He will remove for him his misdeeds and make great for him his reward (5) (At-Talaq) And now, a question: Isn't it only the one who fears Allah for whom He makes a way out! And I am not one of the God-fearing!? Not so! For He has said that whoever avoids what He forbids, obeys His commands and turns to Him in repentance enters the ranks of the God-fearing; on top of that, He removes his misdeeds, and beyond that, He makes his reward great, because He replaces bad deeds with good (and whoever fears Allah - He will remove for him his misdeeds and make great for him his reward (5) Turning the hard into the easy is part of His command and His decree, sent down from heaven to earth. Read the two verses — and please, take your time and look closely at the link between them! — (And whoever fears Allah - He will make for him of his matter ease (4) That is the command of Allah, which He has sent down to you) That is the command of Allah, which He has sent down to you: the rulings on divorce set out earlier in the surah, and all that Allah has ordained.
