Now reflect with me: whoever obeys Allah's command, Allah makes his own matter easy for him! For the reward is of the same kind as the deed (be as He wants, and He will be for you as you want). Obey His command, and He will ease your affair and keep His promise to you; for the fulfillment of Allah's promise of victory and opening is conditional on obedience and the avoidance of sin. Yes! He makes his hard matter easy — that is the command of Allah! Don't ask how!? Impossible? It is His command, and that is that. (Lodge them [in a section] of where you dwell out of your means and do not harm them in order to oppress them. And if they should be pregnant, then spend on them until they give birth. And if they breastfeed for you, then give them their payment and confer among yourselves in the acceptable way; but if you are in discord, then there may breastfeed for the father another woman (6) At-Talaq And this verse too, as I see it, closes with a promise of ease! Where? (but if you are in discord): if you cannot agree on the mother — the divorced wife — nursing the child, Allah will make another nursing woman easy to find! (then there may breastfeed for the father another woman) — provided you fear Allah and act on what comes at the start of the verse: the lodging and the other rulings. This is a promise to the child's mother — and to his father too — that nursing will be made easy, so do not carry the worry Then He promises ease, too, to the man anxious over how little he has in hand (Let a man of wealth spend from his wealth, and he whose provision is restricted - let him spend from what Allah has given him. Allah does not charge a soul except [according to] what He has given it. Allah will bring about, after hardship, ease (7) (And how many a city was insolent toward the command of its Lord and His messengers, so We took it to severe account and punished it with a terrible punishment (8) And it tasted the bad consequence of its affair, and the outcome of its affair was loss (9) Allah has prepared for them a severe punishment; so fear Allah, O you of understanding who have believed. Allah has sent down to you the Qur'an (10) (At-Talaq) When it defied Allah and His Messenger, it met a severe reckoning and punishment in this world; so whoever wants protection from that must hold fast to the fear of Allah — and that is why He said (so fear Allah, O you of understanding who have believed. Allah has sent down to you the Qur'an) If you want ease in your affairs and your provision, and hardship to lift, then hold fast to taqwa; and if taqwa is hard for you, then hold fast to reciting the Quran, for it eases the means of attaining it. The Quran and taqwa are two helpers in hardship, and through them affairs are made easy — the Quran your Messenger ﷺ recites ([He sent] a Messenger [Muhammad] reciting to you the distinct verses of Allah that He may bring out those who believe and do righteous deeds from darknesses into the light. And whoever believes in Allah and does righteousness - He will admit him into gardens beneath which rivers flow to abide therein forever. Allah will have perfected for him a provision (11) The Quran brings him out of the darknesses into the light, and through it his provision in this world and the Hereafter is made good (Allah will have perfected for him a provision) Surah At-Talaq is a wonder! It sets out the rulings of divorce, with all the brokenness, hardship and pain divorce carries! And through it all, the surah scatters rays of hope and joy, promising ease after hardship, and good provision! What is this exquisite beauty in this surah?! Tell me, by your Lord, what is this splendor?! It breaks through the dark, gloomy mood when souls have grown troubled and darkened, promising them ample provision, hope, goodness and ease! Promising that however great the trial, what is coming is more beautiful than what is, and than anything you imagine. It is as if it breaks divorce with rays of radiance

t: Good Tidings in Times of Hardship
x: You see this idea everywhere: that good tidings will not come while your heart is full of fear (And when the fright had left Abraham and the good tidings had reached him) You see this idea everywhere: that good tidings will not come while your heart is full of fear (And when the fright had left Abraham and the good tidings had reached him) How glad I am of anyone who reflects on the Quran! But sound reflection is built on a sound understanding of the Quran. For the verse means this: Abraham (peace be upon him) felt apprehension toward his guests; then they told him they were angels sent to the people of Lot; then they gave him the good tidings of Isaac and Jacob (peace be upon them) So the meaning is: the fright left him once they had given him the good tidings of Isaac and Jacob. Besides, feelings are not something we are commanded or forbidden; the believer is not called to account for them. In fact, good tidings come most often in times of hardship, fear, pain and grief. The Quran is full of this, like the good tidings given to the Messenger ﷺ and the believers in their hour of fear (the Battle of Badr), when they were reinforced with angels. For in times of fear a person needs good tidings to steady his heart far more than he does in times of ease! Read these verses slowly; don't let your eye skim past them. You will see that good tidings come in the hour of fear, to make hearts steadfast and to plant feet firmly: ([Remember] when you asked help of your Lord, and He answered you, "Indeed, I will reinforce you with a thousand from the angels, following one another" (9) And Allah made it not but good tidings and so that your hearts would be assured thereby. And victory is not but from Allah. Indeed, Allah is Exalted in Might and Wise (10) [Remember] when He overwhelmed you with drowsiness [giving] security from Him and sent down upon you from the sky, rain by which to purify you and remove from you the evil [suggestions] of Satan and to make steadfast your hearts and plant firmly thereby your feet (11) (Al-Anfal) If that understanding were sound, the good tidings would have been withheld from Abraham (peace be upon him), for he felt from them apprehension ! You were afraid? Then no good tidings for you!! No, this understanding does not hold. So once again: let us read a concise tafsir and understand the verses first, and only then write down our reflections and musings.. Of course, I am the one who needs this advice most of all. Our Lord, increase us in knowledge and in understanding of the Quran.

t: The Art of Answering Blackmail Over the Past (As in the Quran)
x: The past does not cling to a person — not by sacred law, not by reason, not by his present state: this day of yours, and all you live in its new light, is you. The past does not cling to a person — not by sacred law, not by reason, not by his present state: this day of yours, and all you live in its new light, is you. It is people who keep chasing you with it. So it was with Moses, peace be upon him, after he killed the Copt. He left Egypt, then returned to it laden with the message and the divine light, proclaiming to the whole universe that he had changed and turned toward the light, and that he would change the world along with him — from harshness and cruelty to the light of prophethood, to forbearance and compassion {And speak to him with gentle speech}. Then Pharaoh pursues him with his past before ever pursuing him with his soldiers {And [then] you did your deed which you did, and you are of the disbelievers (19) ! You lay claim to light, to a message, to guidance — and forget that you killed one of us! Reflect on Moses' reply, peace be upon him, and you see that he admitted it in one very short sentence, for the past does not deserve long-winded argument in answer {[Moses] said, "I did it, then, while I was of those astray} — Let me correct you, Pharaoh! First of all, I am not one of the disbelievers; I was a believer, but that deed was a straying. To face blackmail over your past means correcting the other's error and injustice in the way he describes you; for he may blow a small thing out of all proportion because of the great rancor and malice he bears you, so he wrongs you, his descriptions run riot, and his words and insults turn vile: “Abusing a Muslim is Fusuq (an evil doing).” So the first thing to do is correct those descriptions and refuse to accept them; then make plain the truth of what happened and what your own part was, without denial — for the scout does not lie to his people. And last of all, one very brief sentence to answer every blackmail over the past; for Moses, peace be upon him, had before him tasks far greater and weightier than a case long dead and done. What has passed and gone does not deserve elaboration. And I picture Moses, peace be upon him, giving his answer with calm, serenity and confidence; the proof is that he at once confronted Pharaoh with Pharaoh's own past: {And is this a favor of which you remind me — that you have enslaved the Children of Israel?} Tell me, by your Lord: which crime is greater — killing a soul by mistake, or slaughtering the little boys of the Children of Israel, guilty of nothing!? And which is greater: sowing division among them, or killing a soul by mistake? {And fitnah is greater than killing} {and made its people into factions} — Pharaoh split the Children of Israel into factions so that they would quarrel among themselves, for fear they might come to rule Egypt. And which crime is graver: killing a soul, and then a soul filled with remorse, lowliness and brokenness {He said, "My Lord, forgive me," and He forgave him}, with an abiding sense of guilt that drives it to seek forgiveness and to pour itself out in prayer in the hours before dawn {He said, "My Lord, indeed, I killed from among them someone}! Or killing souls and lives and seizing homes in arrogance and haughtiness {And indeed, Pharaoh was haughty within the land, and indeed, he was of the transgressors}? Is the one who killed without restraint, and on purpose, like one who killed a single soul by mistake! There is no comparison! And then, set all this aside: is the sin of one who stood upon light from his Lord the same as the sin of one steeped in disbelief and polytheism! And is one who sinned and then came out of the darkness of misguidance into the light of guidance the same as one who abides forever in his darkness {and are given to drink scalding water that will sever their intestines!} Moses did not keep silent before Pharaoh's blackmail over his past; he answered, silenced him, demolished his claims and took back his due from him {[Moses] said, "I did it, then, while I was of those astray. So I fled from you when I feared you. Then my Lord granted me wisdom and prophethood and appointed me [as one] of the messengers. And is this a favor of which you remind me — that you have enslaved the Children of Israel?} Once he had corrected Pharaoh's descriptions and made his admission, he went on to speak of Allah's favor upon him, to take back his due from Pharaoh and his lying claims: that he was a believing messenger, graced by Allah with the message and the light — proclaiming that he had changed and was no longer the man he had been. And he went on telling him of Allah's favor and bounty upon him, far greater than your favor, Pharaoh! It is Allah's favor, not yours to hold over me, and you have no right to hold it over me {[Pharaoh] said, "Did we not raise you among us as a child, and you remained among us for years of your life?}! And what favor is this that you hold over me — enslaving the Children of Israel? Do you truly see it as a favor, that you enslave the Children of Israel and kill them? What is this favor of yours beside Allah's favor upon me of light and revelation? Moses, peace be upon him, met Pharaoh's reproaches with weightier arguments that left him speechless; he could not answer them, and fell silent! Then off he went, opening another subject, hoping to find a way out! {Said Pharaoh, "And what is the Lord of the worlds?"}. And among the prophets is one who kept silent before his people's blackmail over his past and left it unanswered, out of nobility and patient endurance {They said, "If he steals — a brother of his has stolen before." But Joseph kept it within himself and did not reveal it to them} until the moment of complete victory should come; for that is a mightier reply and a more crushing answer than quick retorts and side battles {They said, "By Allah, certainly has Allah preferred you over us, and indeed, we have been sinners."} — We sinned twice: first when we threw you into the well, and again when we called you a thief, to your face, while you were providing for us out of charity. By Allah, you are no thief, for a thief is not honored: “He whom Thou takest as an enemy is not honored, and he whom Thou befriendest is not humbled” {My Lord, You have given me [something] of sovereignty and taught me of the interpretation of dreams. Creator of the heavens and earth, You are my protector in this world and in the Hereafter} But the soul chafes at words like these, and some reply there must be; so he deferred his reply for a long while, and kept it hidden for a short while. As for the short delay: he answered them within himself {He said, "You are worse in position, and Allah is most knowing of what you describe."} — and a reply within the soul is still a reply and an answer; whoever answers an opponent within himself has given himself his due. Allah knows best who is the thief, who the abductor, and who the wrongdoer. One who was dressed in his father's belt as a little child who understood nothing is not the equal of those who, as grown men, snatched a small boy and flung him to the bottom of a well without mercy; and those who plotted murder are not like one accused of theft who never stole at all {Kill Joseph}. Murder is the graver crime, and throwing him into the well was nothing but a way to be rid of him. (The theft that Joseph's brothers attributed to him, according to Ibn Kathir: that he stole an idol and broke it. It is also said that he never stole at all: rather, when his aunt, the daughter of Isaac, wanted to keep Joseph with her out of love for him, she fastened around him the girdle (belt) of Isaac, peace be upon him, which they used to pass down as an heirloom; then she said, “Search for it,” and they found it on Joseph, and so they said Joseph had stolen. And he is innocent of this) As for deferring the reply a long while: he returned it to them in the next-to-last scene of the story {He said, "Do you know what you did with Joseph and his brother when you were ignorant?"}!? Yes: the past for the past, blackmail for blackmail, and for wounds is legal retribution! But it takes intelligence to hold back the reply until a moment when the opponent has neither answer nor argument — so he is silenced, finished, and he apologizes and confesses {They said, "By Allah, certainly has Allah preferred you over us, and indeed, we have been sinners."} We are the sinners, not you. The small offense fades and is swallowed up in the great one, so the one with the greater crime apologizes, and the honorable son of the honorable forgives, and Allah honors him and raises his standing. Let no one's provocation over your past drive you to abandon the insight and the message you carry; for it is one of life's trials that a servant be exposed to people's ill thoughts of him (And We have made some of you [people] as trial for others — will you have patience?) So be patient. Indeed, the promise of Allah is truth. And let them not disquiet you who are not certain [in faith] (60) So take care: do not let their provocation push you into folly, flightiness and recklessness ( wa lā yastakhiffannaka , “let them not disquiet you”: let them not provoke you); rather, stand confident upon the guidance and proof you hold.

t: The Likeness of Affliction
x: Imagine with me a rope drawn tight around your chest, and drawn with wisdom. Imagine with me a rope drawn tight around your chest, and drawn with wisdom. You hold your ground, and it tightens; your chest grows narrower, and narrower still, and then, all at once, it snaps! Such is affliction. It tightens around you until your chest is straitened by it, but the moment it sees fortitude and patience in you, it snaps. (Indeed, We found him patient): We found him, in every trial, patient and seeking his reward from Allah. But if you buckle, twisting right and left in panic and resentment, the rope slackens around you, only to draw tight again before long; it never snaps, and you never slip free.

t: The Enchantment of Repetition
x: If there were one way to prove the truth of the Quran, and the soundness of every vowel and every letter in it, that way would be repetition! If there were one way to prove the truth of the Quran, and the soundness of every vowel and every letter in it, that way would be repetition! Why? Because when words are repeated, we can tell a lying speaker from a truthful one; this is how his contradictions come to light Say (A) tells us: I was in Riyadh on Saturday Then tells someone else: I was at home on Saturday. The repeated sentence, with its single meaning, "I was… on Saturday," has handed us a glaring contradiction between Riyadh and home, and from it we understand that he is lying to us. Yes, perhaps he simply forgot his first lie; which is why they say: if one day you decide to lie, you had better have a good memory;) And the liar does forget his lies, for human memory is frail whether he likes it or not, and the passing days and changing times give him away. Had this Quranic repetition come from a human being, we would have found in it contradictions almost beyond counting; for it is human nature to forget one's earlier contradictory sentence (A) while uttering the later one (B) (If it had been from [any] other than Allah, they would have found within it much contradiction (82) (An-Nisa) And it is repetition that brings such contradictions to light! How else do we know that a questionnaire in a research study has been answered falsely? From the repeated answers! I mean: if every question in a questionnaire carried a completely different idea, we could never tell the truthful respondent from the liar. One and the same question has to be repeated in more than one wording, so the researcher can tell the truthful from the liar: Take, for instance, questions three and sixteen of a questionnaire measuring overconsumption: 3- On weekends I never spend my money 16- On Saturdays my children and I go out to a restaurant. The two questions, you see, carry one and the same meaning; if someone answers "agree" to both, it is clear he is lying, and so the questionnaire is spoiled and goes straight into the bin. Now let us return to repetition in the Quran. We have given evidence that Allah the Exalted placed repetition and the resembling verses there deliberately and with wisdom, not in vain: to prove that it is sent down from Allah. And nothing reveals to the human mind that it is from Allah the way repetition does. Had the Quran been made up entirely of topics wholly distinct from one another (with no repetition, that is), its truthfulness would never have become clear to us, and it would be like any other man-made book! For it is in books composed by humans that every chapter brings us a new idea, and the author varies his styles throughout. True, some human books repeat certain ideas and phrases. A cookbook, for example, will repeat the phrase (3/4 cup of water) in different contexts, but always with the same meaning! The Quran is altogether different! Even its repetition gives us two things: 1- a shared meaning 2- a further meaning added to the shared one. Let us take an example of the resembling verses: Of Yusuf (peace be upon him): (And when Joseph reached maturity, We gave him judgment and knowledge. And thus We reward the doers of good (22) (Yusuf) Of Musa (peace be upon him): (And when he attained his full strength and was [mentally] mature, We bestowed upon him judgement and knowledge. And thus do We reward the doers of good (14) (Al-Qasas) Both share a single meaning: ( ātaynāhu ḥukman wa-ʿilmā , We gave him judgment and knowledge), which is prophethood, for both were prophets. The difference, however, is that "( wa-stawā , and was mature) expresses Musa's bodily strength (peace be upon him), whereas Yusuf (peace be upon him) was beautiful" - Dr. Fadil al-Samarrai And such distinctions between the meanings of repeated phrases are lost on a Frenchman or an Englishman (with apologies); it takes someone skilled in Arabic, gifted in it, to uncover such fine linguistic differences, or at the very least someone who has learned its rudiments. So no one unlearned in Arabic, whatever his academic standing, has any right to object to the Quran's repetitions until he has gone deep into Arabic and mastered it; then let us hear his opinion again! For the heights of reflection are reached only by one who has mastered Arabic, grasped its secrets, and tasted its eloquence and its literature. Repetition is everywhere in nature! Think of the petals of a flower, matching in shape and number, in perfect regularity. This orderly, harmonious repetition of a single element is, first of all, the source of beauty. Imagine one flower with a single petal and the next with three! Like mangled teeth: one broken, the next pulled out, a third worn down to a quarter, a fourth to a third! How ugly the sight, how the eye recoils from it. But when every flower has five petals, that is what captivates us, and we exclaim: Allah! How beautiful! Repetition is also the source of benefit: because flowers and petals repeat, the bees can benefit from them, so there is work for everyone! Isn't that so? Were they irregular, there would be fights and grinding battles, honey production would fall, the bees would starve, and the sick would be slower to heal. In the same way, repetition in the Quran is one of the sources of healing: certain verses recur in more than one place, and this recurrence is itself a means of healing, such as the verses of provision, the verses of affection, the verses of tranquility, the verses on magic, and others. So when the whole Quran passes over your tongue and through your heart, from al-Fatiha to an-Nas, and you complete it, that is the fullest healing, and brings more provision and blessing than confining yourself to a single surah. That is why you should be keen to complete it each time (at least once a month). There is no harm in repeating one particular surah, such as al-Baqarah, every day; but be keen to complete the whole as well, say, a full reading every two weeks and al-Baqarah every day. Wonderful! This is what has given the Quran its beauty and its absolute order, so that jinn and humans together cannot produce its like! It comes from the splendor of its repetition and the enchantment of its weave. It is density that brings the rain! A single cloud on its own does nothing; only when clouds gather, one upon another, does the rain fall. That is why the singular ( saḥābah , a cloud) never appears in the Quran! It always comes in the plural (the heavy clouds) ( saḥāban ), for saḥāb (“clouds”) is the plural of saḥābah (“a cloud”). Likewise, it is these resembling verses and repetitions that make the Quran heavy; and the Quran, as is well known, is heavy (Indeed, We will cast upon you a heavy word (5) And this very heaviness is what brings the heart to life through the Quran! Like dead land that will not bloom except under heavy clouds and dense rain. What makes the Quran heavy, then, is its repetition and its resembling verses, and they are why it is the rain by which Allah revives hearts after their death, and the heart turns to springtime 🌿 Were it empty of repetition, there would be no difference between the heart before reading and after! Without repetition, it would stay dead. And whoever kept company with the heavy word in this world will be among the lightest of people in the Hereafter, in reckoning and in standing (Indeed, these [disbelievers] love the immediate and leave behind them a grave Day ( yawman thaqīlā ) (27) (Al-Insan) Imagine a natural world whose elements were all distinct from one another; or say: a world with no repetition at all .. how do you picture it? I picture it monotonous, dull, ugly, shallow, with nothing in it worth pondering or putting the mind to work on! Were it not for repetition, reflecting on the Quran would not be possible; it would be impossible! (Then do they not reflect upon the Qur'an? If it had been from [any] other than Allah, they would have found within it much contradiction (82) (An-Nisa) It is repetition that stirs the question in you: what is the difference between the verses about Musa and Pharaoh in al-A'raf and in ash-Shu'ara? Why are the sentences different? And so you dive deeper and deeper into meanings, suppositions and possibilities! Why is ( thumma , then) added here, and the fā' (“so”) added there? And why does this verse have the fā' while that one does without it, when it is the very same story? This is what makes the Quran a delightful journey of thought and reflection that goes on as human beings grow. If they reflected on all of it, they would never reach the end of its inexhaustible wonders, and it would pour out to them its sciences and the secrets of Arabic,, if only they took hold of it earnestly and firmly, and made it a lifelong quest of the mind called: the quest of reflection, for all of life and all of the journey. So I cannot imagine the life of a learned, cultured person without reflection on the Quran at the very top of their pursuit of knowledge! This is for the believer, and for the deep believer who grasps this meaning.

t: Connection Before Correction!
x: Connect with the child first: show him your love, for instance, and your encouragement, and ask him about his day. Only then give your direct advice! Connect with the child first: show him your love, for instance, and your encouragement, and ask him about his day. Only then give your direct advice! The Messenger of Allah ﷺ caught his hand and said: By Allah, I love you, Mu'adh. I give some instruction to you. Never leave to recite this supplication after every (prescribed) prayer: "O Allah, help me in remembering You, in giving You thanks, and worshipping You well." Notice how, in this hadith, he ﷺ expressed his love first (connection), and only then began to guide. Don't correct in the heat of a strong outburst Calm him first, then correct. The mind cannot take in what is said to it in the grip of fierce anger; this is a time not for teaching, but for soothing.

t: With Your Children, Don't Be the Preacher
x: With your children, don't be the preacher while they sit as your audience, as though you were Richard the war orator! With your children, don't be the preacher while they sit as your audience, as though you were Richard the war orator! Instead, turn the sermon into a conversation you share: questions and answers, back-and-forth, a few brief words from you, and listening. That is how the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was. Look at his hadiths and you will find that most of them are dialogues, though he could simply have poured his words into the listener's ear and walked on! But he knew that what we share and talk through together stays longer in the mind, and shows more respect for the person in front of us, who is a human being, not a wall to drone at. And question and answer also tells the one in front of you that you love to hear him speak. "I was a companion rider of the Prophet ﷺ on a donkey. He said, 'O Mu'adh! Do you know what Allah's right on His slaves is, and what the right of His slaves on Him is?' I replied, 'Allah and His Apostle know better.' He said, 'Allah's right on His slaves is that they should worship Him (Alone) and should not worship any besides Him. And slave's right on Allah is that He should not punish him who worships none besides Him.'"

t: The Sun in (Al-A'la, At-Tin, Ash-Shams, Al-Layl, and Ad-Duha)
x: There is a complete and perfect harmony between Surat Al-A'la, Ash-Shams and Al-Layl: each moves step by step from the creation of the heavens and the earth, to the creation of man, to the human soul, which then splits into two kinds according to how it strives to purify itself; then come the two paths, guidance and misguidance, laid out plainly, and where each path leads in this world and the Hereafter. There is a complete and perfect harmony between Surat Al-A'la, Ash-Shams and Al-Layl: each moves step by step from the creation of the heavens and the earth, to the creation of man, to the human soul, which then splits into two kinds according to how it strives to purify itself; then come the two paths, guidance and misguidance, laid out plainly, and where each path leads in this world and the Hereafter. Except that Surat Al-A'la is broader than Ash-Shams, and Ash-Shams broader than Surat Al-Layl, while Surat Ad-Duha is narrower than both, and At-Tin narrower still. So look with me — may Allah let you long enjoy your sight: (Surat Al-A'la) Exalt the name of your Lord, the Most High (1) Who created and proportioned (2) And who destined and [then] guided (3) (Surat Ash-Shams) By the sun and its brightness (1) And [by] the moon when it follows it (2) And [by] the day when it displays it (3) And [by] the night when it covers it (4) And [by] the sky and He who constructed it (5) And [by] the earth and He who spread it (6) And [by] the soul and He who proportioned it (7) And inspired it [with discernment of] its wickedness and its righteousness (8) He has succeeded who purifies it (9) And he has failed who instills it [with corruption] (10). (Surat Al-Layl) By the night when it covers (1) And [by] the day when it appears (2) And [by] He who created the male and female (3) Indeed, your efforts are diverse (4) In Surat Al-A'la He shows us the Creator behind all creation, and so it opens by glorifying and exalting Him. Then comes His creating of everything — heavens and earth, animals, humans and plants — in that He proportioned each in the finest form, then destined for it its measures and provisions, or set them in the very nature of its making, and then guided it. So it is the most general of them, embracing every creation and every kind of guidance — so much so that He guides the ant as it carries a grain on its back. And in Surat Ash-Shams He begins with the creation of the day and the night, the sun and the moon, the sky and the earth, then the creation of the soul and its kinds, and tells us that its purpose is to strive to perfect it and to attain its righteousness. And Surat Al-Layl follows the very same pattern: in these surahs there is a marvelous order, even in time and in history — the creation of the heavens and the earth, then the creation of man and his soul, and then the purpose of creation: his striving toward guidance, and the truth that the soul can reach no perfection except by bringing its guidance to perfection. Taghshiyah (covering) and tasjiyah (shrouding): In Ash-Shams and Al-Layl, He describes the night as covering (And [by] the night when it covers it) (By the night when it covers). And in Ad-Duha He uses tasjiyah (And [by] the night when it covers with darkness — idhā sajā ). And the reason — and Allah knows best — is that ghishā' is used for a complete and total covering, while tasjiyah is used for intensity, and it was borrowed here for the night to show how intense that hour is. Astronomers tell us that when evening falls, the sun has not fully set! It does not fully set until 8 p.m., and in some countries not until eleven at night, and this varies with winter and summer and from one country to another. So the meaning may be: when the night covers, as the sun vanishes from it entirely — not merely its apparent setting to the naked eye. And when the day appears, as the moon vanishes entirely from the daytime sky. So it speaks of the day in its fullness and the night in its fullness, each set truly apart from the other, not as the eye mistakenly sees them. As for tasjiyah : it comes from binding the shroud tightly around the dead, wrapping him in cloth and covering. For the dead may be covered and fully shrouded, and yet not tightly bound and fastened. And so (And [by] the night when it covers with darkness) is the night at its deepest, near its end, in the hour before dawn. Here the marvelous astronomical order of the surahs becomes clear to you! They move within an orderly, precise orbit of time: Surat Ash-Shams and Al-Layl open with night and day fully covered — say it is eleven o'clock — and Surat Ad-Duha with the late hours of the night, around three in the morning, for example. Except that the meaning of Surat Ad-Duha is that it reveals the most intense hours for purifying and refining the soul, as though Surat Ash-Shams poses a riddle: how is the soul purified, and when? And Surat Ad-Duha answers: when the hour is at its most intense! These are the voluntary prayers: the voluntary prayer of the day is the Duha prayer, and the voluntary prayer of the night is more effective for concurrence [of heart and tongue] and more suitable for words. A heavy load can only be moved by something as heavy or heavier; it makes no sense to tow a broken-down truck with a flimsy bicycle! That is sheer folly. No — true wisdom is to bring a truck like it, or a heavier one, to tow it, get it moving and bring it back to life; and so it is with the soul, weighed down by desires — the very things that stall a person and keep him from moving swiftly and lightly, and shut him off from goodness and blessing. So something heavier than the soul had to lead it, and that was the two revelations, the Quran and the Sunnah (Allah wants to accept your repentance, but those who follow [their] passions want you to digress [into] a great deviation (27) And Allah wants to lighten for you [your difficulties]; and mankind was created weak (28) (An-Nisa) Lighten what for us? The very passions you read about in the verse before it! And it is absurd to rely on the self alone to straighten and correct it, with man-made Western methods and programs; that is a bicycle towing a truck! Either the rope between them snaps, or the cyclist's back gives way and breaks. The ways of the Quran and the Sunnah are indispensable for changing the human soul, alongside human research and methods, Western or Eastern, when their ideas are balanced and sound — they complement one another — except that the two revelations are heavier, and better. We said that the night and the day are meant in their fullness, as they arrive and in their own time; (And [by] He who created the male and female) is the same: just as He told us of the day and the night in their fullness, He goes on to tell us of the creation of male and female in its fullness — each made wholly distinct from the other. Tazkiyah (purifying) and tadsiyah (corrupting) (And [by] the soul and He who proportioned it (7) And inspired it [with discernment of] its wickedness and its righteousness (8) He has succeeded who purifies it (9) And he has failed who instills it [with corruption] (10) We said that He perfected the creation of the night and the day, and the bodily make-up of male and female; and He also perfected the creation of the human soul, granting it the gift of thought and feeling, proportioning it in the finest proportion, wronging it in nothing. Yet it remains for man to complete his soul and set it right, until its darkness stands apart from its light — and that is by leading it, along the path of purification, out of the darknesses and into the clear light! By earnest, wholehearted striving toward guidance (Indeed, your efforts are diverse) — and sa'y , striving, is faster than walking, as if He were saying: if you could gain guidance in a single day and night, then hurry to it! Of course that is impossible; it is only because guidance and righteousness matter so much, so that his creation may be made complete by the completeness of his character — and this is the trust man is bound to fulfill. Just as He perfected the creation of the heavens and the earth for you, and perfected your own creation in the finest form, the repayment for this divine goodness is that you complete the purification of your soul and bring your righteousness to perfection (Is the reward for good [anything] but good?). The wretched soul and the happy soul Thamud denied [their prophet] by reason of their transgression (11) When the most wretched of them was sent forth (12) And the messenger of Allah [Salih] said to them, "[Do not harm] the she-camel of Allah or [prevent her from] her drink" (13) But they denied him and hamstrung her. So their Lord brought down upon them destruction for their sin and made it equal [upon all of them] (14) And He does not fear the consequence thereof (15). Having set out the divisions of the happy and the wretched soul (And he has failed who instills it [with corruption]), He gives a real example of one particular wretched soul: the most wretched of the people of Thamud — showing that this is the end of whoever does not strive for guidance and purify himself: his own soul leads him astray, until it trips him, seduces him, and drives him to transgress. And if you ask me: why does Surat Ash-Shams tell the story of Thamud, and not, say, of Pharaoh, who was more wretched than him? The surah is brief, so brevity suits it, and one example suffices of the wretched soul that would not be purified — and of how whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger meets such an end in this world, before the Hereafter. And why does He not give an example of the happy soul that was purified? It is in the nature of the human mind that when we hold two opposite ideas, an example of the worse lets us grasp the example of the better on our own — and this is intelligence, eloquence, and the art of saying much in little. The happy soul and the wretched soul: if I give you an example of the wretched soul and where it ends up, you will understand the happy soul and its end without being told. And the meaning is: if this is the end of the wretched soul in this world, before the Hereafter, then likewise the happy soul — the one that purified itself, strove for guidance, and obeyed Allah and His Messenger — finds happiness in this world before the Hereafter. And if you ask me: if He has shown the worldly punishment of wretchedness, where is the punishment of the Hereafter!? We say that He has shown it in Surat Al-A'la: But the wretched one will avoid it (11) [He] who will [enter and] burn in the greatest Fire (12) Neither dying therein nor living (13) He has certainly succeeded who purifies himself (14) And mentions the name of his Lord and prays (15). So the traits of the wretched soul are set out in detail in Ash-Shams (When the most wretched of them was sent forth), and his recompense in the Hereafter is made plain in Surat Al-A'la (But the wretched one will avoid it). That is why Surat Al-A'la is broader than Ash-Shams. That whoever does not put his wretched self to death here, by striving and struggle, and bring the good self to life through purification, giving it a noble and goodly life, and does not believe in the best [reward], will have a Fire in which he neither dies nor lives; and whoever brings his soul to life by keeping the night alive with the Quran and voluntary prayer will have two lives = which together make one good life, in this world and the Hereafter, and his life is worth the life of a whole nation, (And whoever saves one - it is as if he had saved mankind entirely); and what gives the soul life but the Quran and standing in prayer at night? So He promises success in this world and the Hereafter to the one who purifies his soul; and zakāh includes the meaning of purifying souls, as Ibn Kathir mentioned in his exegesis of verse 156 of Surat Al-A'raf). From this we may glean that ṣadaqah (charity) — and Allah knows best — shares in the meaning of taṣdīq (believing) and ṣiddīq (the truthful one). But you prefer the worldly life (16) While the Hereafter is better and more enduring (17) Indeed, this is in the former scriptures (18) The scriptures of Abraham and Moses (19) (Al-A'la) And since some souls doubt these words — that Allah has a sure and unchanging way of correcting, straightening and guiding the soul — He sealed the surah with what the soul trusts most firmly: writing, scriptures, history. These are Allah's ways of straightening and balancing souls and making life good — so much so that He mentioned them in the scriptures of Abraham (peace be upon him) and the Torah of Moses (peace be upon him); and just as it is told there, it is told again here in the Quran, to affirm this truth and principle, so that you may be certain that the truest way of changing a human being toward the highest and most complete is the Quran and the Sunnah and all they hold (So if you are in doubt, [O Muhammad], about that which We have revealed to you, then ask those who have been reading the Scripture before you. The truth has certainly come to you from your Lord, so never be among the doubters (94) So the scriptures were not mentioned for the sake of rhyme — far be it — but for whoever doubts these ways and laws, just as you would say to someone who doubts your word: if you don't believe me, ask so-and-so; he can bear witness to what I say. (Surat At-Tin) By the fig and the olive (1) And [by] Mount Sinai (2) And [by] this secure city [Makkah] (3) We have certainly created man in the best of stature (4) Then We return him to the lowest of the low (5) Except for those who believe and do righteous deeds, for they will have a reward uninterrupted (6) So what yet causes you to deny the Recompense (7) Is not Allah the most just of judges (8). Like the pairs of night and day, male and female, the wretched soul and the happy one, here too He pairs the fig with the olive; and what is the link!? If the reach of man's senses toward the sun and the moon is sight alone, the fig and the olive lie within reach of every sense, even the two most intimate: smell and taste — and that may be the meaning intended here! The fig tastes sweet, and the olive tastes bitter. And so the pair is complete: bitterness and sweetness — the human soul tastes its straying as bitterness, pain and misery, and tastes its guidance as the sweetness of faith, joy and delight. And Mount Sinai: because there He revealed the Torah to Moses (peace be upon him). And this secure city: because revelation came down in it, and because Abraham (peace be upon him) built the Kaaba there, may Allah exalt it. These two places were honored only because revelation came down in them — so what of a heart into which the Quran came down, and which held it in memory, lived by it and understood it! Would it not be the most honored of hearts and the most complete of souls! We have certainly created man in the best of stature: in body and in soul, yet there are flaws and stains in it (Then We return him to the lowest of the low) — except for whoever purifies it and cleanses it of them. The most just of judges: the real question of divine decree is not why Allah enriched this one and gave that one sufficiency — much of that we can understand — but why He guided this one and let that one go astray. So He pointed us to the truth that decree belongs to Him (And who destined and [then] guided), for all judgment and all knowledge are His; and just as we have accepted the other questions of decree, we must accept this one too. Do you not see that Noah (peace be upon him) called upon his Lord by this very name (And Noah called to his Lord and said, "My Lord, indeed my son is of my family; and indeed, Your promise is true; and You are the most just of judges" (45) (Hud) So the Most Just of Judges guides whom He wills and leaves astray whom He wills. The secret of perfect contentment [He] who gives [from] his wealth to purify himself (18) And not [giving] for anyone who has [done him] a favor to be rewarded (19) But only seeking the countenance of his Lord, Most High (20) And he is going to be satisfied (21).(Al-Layl) And your Lord is going to give you, and you will be satisfied (5) (Ad-Duha) Sincerity in private worship is easy, but in worship that involves others, and above all in giving, it is very hard — except for those Allah makes it easy for. So there must be sincerity in giving: give for Allah, and hold back for Allah; whoever chases people's approval with his giving burns himself out and dies of sorrow. We have found nothing more restful to the soul than giving for Allah, because that is what brings you contentment. And the Quran says this again and again: And the example of those who spend their wealth seeking means to the approval of Allah … (265) Al-Baqarah No good is there in much of their private conversation, except for those who enjoin charity or that which is right or conciliation between people. And whoever does that seeking means to the approval of Allah - then We are going to give him a great reward (114) (An-Nisa) All of these are good deeds done toward people, and so He made clear that whoever seeks to please Allah, not people, will have a great reward: Allah's pleasure with him, and provision and gifts poured upon him until he is content; for the recompense matches the deed — he gave only to seek the pleasure of Allah, so his recompense is that Allah gives to him until He has made him content, and his soul is at peace. (And who brings out the pasture (4) And [then] makes it black stubble (5) We will make you recite, [O Muhammad], and you will not forget (6) Except what Allah should will. Indeed, He knows what is declared and what is hidden (7) And We will ease you toward ease (8).(Al-A'la) (And who brings out the pasture and [then] makes it black stubble) fits this world and its passing states, but that is not the state of one who recites the Quran: he lives in an endless spring — which is why it is followed by (We will make you recite, [O Muhammad], and you will not forget) And this is the secret behind the words of the Chosen One ﷺ: "O Allah, make the Quran the spring of my heart" — he did not say the plant of my heart, or its flower! For these wither, while spring is a season that lasts through days and months. And whoever keeps carrying the Quran is always in this state: in a joy that never breaks off and a gladness that never fades. Then He makes clear His knowledge of what is declared and what is hidden of the soul's secret schemings; and so Surat Al-A'la is general, and Surat Ash-Shams narrower than it, and so on with the rest of the surahs. (But as for the favor of your Lord, report [it]) They are all favors, except the Quran: (the favor of your Lord) — an attribution of honor and glory to the Mighty Lord. You are not, [O Muhammad], by the favor of your Lord, a madman (2) So remind [O Muhammad], for you are not, by the favor of your Lord, a soothsayer or a madman (29) And the difference between the favor of the Lord and the favor of Allah: Ask the Children of Israel how many a sign of evidence We have given them. And whoever exchanges the favor of Allah [for disbelief] after it has come to him - then indeed, Allah is severe in penalty (211) This was revealed about the Children of Israel And whoever exchanges the favor of Allah: those who altered and distorted the Torah and the Gospel and turned away from them, abandoning this favor for the little of this world (and all that is in this world is little); but He said "the favor of Allah," using the Name of Majesty to threaten, to warn and to rebuke. And the favor of your Lord: to show tenderness and to put the heart at ease. And the favor of your Lord: for the paths to salvation, guidance, light and happiness in this world and the Hereafter that it holds.

t: Raising a Child Is Not the Same as Indulging One
x: True upbringing is supportive and responsible, never indulgent. True upbringing is supportive and responsible, never indulgent. Pampering and indulgence mean saying yes to everything: no limits where the child must stop, no discipline, money showered on him, and every wish granted. Supportive upbringing, by contrast, meets his emotional and social needs (connection, understanding, empathy, a listening ear) without always meeting his material demands! And in the very same moment, it means discipline, boundaries, and, at times, saying no. Why saying no is good for a child: - He learns to delay gratification, which sharpens his willpower and patience - It helps him think about how to get what he wants, so he strives and works for it. - It teaches him empathy, so he can feel what it is to go without, as others do. Excessive pampering, on the other hand, builds a weak and brittle character, one that takes no responsibility for its actions and leans on others. When a child pours out his anger and sorrow to the one raising him, and that person listens, understands and holds him close, this is part of supportive upbringing and has nothing whatsoever to do with indulgence! A child whose parents will not listen pours his feelings out to someone else, and learns from it an unhealthy clinging to others and a constant anxiety. Even if your son is angry and upset in the moment, you soothe his feelings, hold him, pat his shoulders. Not because you are indulgent! But because, right now, you are connecting! The height of anger, the height of tears, is no time for lectures and lessons; he will not take them in. It is a time for support, empathy and calm. Save your lessons for a calmer hour. Sometimes, when connection does not work, you need to say no, show a little anger, be firm with the child and make the limits clear. Then go straight back to making him feel supported. For in doing so you are telling him: I am with you at your worst, even when you have done wrong and angered me; with you to teach, to guide, and to support. In this way you separate the person from the particular behavior.

t: Grace and Courtesy in Listening to the Quran
c: Branches of the Relationship with the Quran
x: She tells me she was lying in a hospital bed, and that the woman beside her turned her Bluetooth speaker up loud with Surah Al-Baqarah and the ruqyah, and that for two, three days she could not sleep because of it. She tells me she was lying in a hospital bed, and that the woman beside her turned her Bluetooth speaker up loud with Surah Al-Baqarah and the ruqyah, and that for two, three days she could not sleep because of it. I told her: that woman has no sense of grace! Perhaps she never heard how he ﷺ would lower his voice with the Quran, for fear of waking his family. And likewise the one who turns the Quran up loud at a traffic light with his window rolled down, forgetting that among people there are those suffering from ear and eye infections and other ailments that sharp, loud sound aggravates, and those with pressing needs, and the elderly. “It has been narrated to us that the Prophet ﷺ heard a man reciting aloud, and he called out to him: O so-and-so, let Allah hear you, and do not make me hear you” (Qut al-Qulub) For no one stands more in need of this Quran's admonitions and warnings than you, O listener, O reciter. As for people, they have a Lord who will guide them; what business is it of yours? Let yourself hear, and set the volume to your own measure, not to the measure of all creation. (And do not recite [too] loudly in your prayer or [too] quietly but seek between that an [intermediate] way (110) (Al-Isra) Reciting aloud means that your own ears hear you. Reciting silently means that you do not hear yourself at all, a mere murmur of the lips. And it used to be said: whatever your ear hears is not silent recitation. “Whoever lets his own ears hear has not recited silently” (al-Tabari) “I was told of a good and pious man who said: I was reciting Surah Ta-Ha before dawn, in a room of mine that opened onto the street, and when I finished it I dozed off. I saw a figure descend from the sky, holding a white scroll, and he spread it out before me; and there was Surah Ta-Ha, and beneath every word ten good deeds were recorded, except for a single word: in its place I saw an erasure, and nothing beneath it. That grieved me, and I said: By Allah, I did recite this word, yet I see no reward for it, nor do I see it recorded! The figure said: You are right, you recited it and we wrote it down for you, but we heard a caller cry out: Erase it, and strike out its reward! So we erased it. I wept in my sleep and said: Why did you do that? They said: A man passed by, and you raised your voice with it for his sake, so we erased it”(Qut al-Qulub) Linguists say that words alone can never express everything in the mind. Even now, as I talk with you and write, there are so many feelings and thoughts these words of mine cannot carry to you; language is not a pipe that delivers everything. Here, I paused the podcast and began to ponder his words ﷺ: “When one of you rises at night to pray, let him use the siwak, for when one of you recites in his prayer, an angel places its mouth upon his mouth, and nothing leaves his mouth but it enters the angel's mouth” (its narrators are trustworthy) Did I perhaps understand, then, why the angel places its mouth upon the reciter's mouth as the Quran is recited? Why not sit at some distance from him, say?! Would that not be enough? I think, though true knowledge is with Allah, that it is because along with the verses it takes in the reciter's thoughts, feelings, intentions, supplications, and requests! It is not merely a matter of taking in the letters; for if it were only the letters, how would the sincere be told apart from the one who shows off? So it takes in everything from the reciter: his intentions, his thoughts, and his feelings as he recites -and Allah knows best-. (And [by] the witness and what is witnessed) Among the meanings I reflected on in this verse: the witness and the witnessed may be the Quran itself. It is a witness for you or against you; it is witnessed in this world, the angels and the believers bear witness to it, and witnessed in the Hereafter, on the day the reciter of the Quran is told: Recite, and rise up. So make it a witness for you, not against you, and do not make it a means of harming people and the sick. Mind public decency and good manners, and let us hold fast to sincerity, for it travels along with our reciting and our listening - and I am the first of those in need of this reminder. O Allah, forgive us, have mercy on us, and grant us sincerity from Yourself-.

t: The Branching Arts of Upbringing in Luqman
x: Educators say that when a child screams, disobeys and rebels, the best thing you can do is: 1- draw close to him physically and rest your hand on the back of his head (this softens him and calms the lower brain, which governs emotions and reactions) 2- then call him by his name (this wins his affection and warmth, so he is readier to accept the message) 3- then tell him the behavior he ought to show. Educators say that when a child screams, disobeys and rebels, the best thing you can do is: 1- draw close to him physically and rest your hand on the back of his head (this softens him and calms the lower brain, which governs emotions and reactions) 2- then call him by his name (this wins his affection and warmth, so he is readier to accept the message) 3- then tell him the behavior he ought to show. It reminded me of the way of the Prophet ﷺ Whenever Aisha grew angry, he would squeeze her nose and say: “O Uwaysh, say: O Allah, Lord of Muhammad, forgive me my sin, take away the rage of my heart, and protect me from the trials that lead astray” (weak) And in one wording: “he took hold of my nose”; he took hold of her nose to calm her. Then he calls her tenderly by the dearest of names (O Uwaysh) (another wording of the hadith has: O Uwayshah, and Aa'ish), and he did not say “O Aisha,” so as to wrap his words in gentleness, warmth, love, charm and playfulness. Had he called her “Aisha,” there might have been a seriousness, an edge, to it; he wanted to soften the words, and the head, completely. Then he tells her what she should do (“say…”), rather than forbidding her what she was doing! Not: don't be angry, let it go, there's no need to make trouble over things that aren't worth it! He goes straight to what he wants her to do. An analysis of Luqman's way of raising his son (peace be upon him): Luqman called his son three times in succession, once before each piece of advice that opened a new subject; yet with prohibition he did not use “O my son” except in one place. We will explain the reasons in their place, Allah willing. More than once he began with command (what ought to be done), then prohibition (what ought not to be done), and this is the soundest of educational methods. And [mention, O Muhammad], when Luqman said to his son while he was instructing him, “O my son, do not associate [anything] with Allah. Indeed, association [with him] is great injustice.” (13) And after the counsel to honor parents, he said: (O my son, indeed if wrong should be the weight of a mustard seed and should be within a rock or [anywhere] in the heavens or in the earth, Allah will bring it forth. Indeed, Allah is Subtle and Acquainted (16) O my son, establish prayer, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and be patient over what befalls you. Indeed, [all] that is of the matters [requiring] determination (17) And do not turn your cheek [in contempt] toward people and do not walk through the earth exultantly. Indeed, Allah does not like everyone self-deluded and boastful (18) And be moderate in your pace and lower your voice; indeed, the most disagreeable of sounds is the voice of donkeys (19) O my son: he says it to be gentle and loving toward his son. Had he called him by his name, there would have been an edge to it that breeds distance, and the counsel would not reach the heart! At most it would reach the mind, where it might stay, or it might go out the other ear. And you can see that all the prophets, peace be upon them, address their children as “my son,” the obedient and the disobedient alike! Noah, peace be upon him: O my son, come aboard with us (42) And Abraham and Jacob, peace be upon them: And Abraham instructed his sons [to do the same] and [so did] Jacob, [saying], “O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen for you this religion, so do not die except while you are Muslims.” (132) Al-Baqarah As for Jacob, peace be upon him, he said it again and again, even to sons who had disobeyed his command and wronged him! (O my sons, go and find out about Joseph and his brother (87) And to Joseph, peace be upon him: (He said, “O my son, do not relate your vision to your brothers (5) And this upbringing shone back from Joseph, peace be upon him, too: he calls to his companions in prison with the gentlest of calls (O [my] two companions of prison, are separate lords better or Allah, the One, the Prevailing? (39) And Abraham with his son Ishmael, peace be upon them: (O my son, indeed I have seen in a dream that I [must] sacrifice you.. (102) Now we return once more to Luqman and his son: With every piece of counsel he put “O my son” first. I see two possibilities, and Allah knows best: 1- Either these were counsels he gave him on different days, which is why he opened each one with “O my son.” Brevity is one of the Quran's rhetorical ways; it is hardly to be expected that it would say with every verse: and on the 11th of such-and-such month, in such-and-such year, at such-and-such hour, Luqman the Wise said…. and on the … of such-and-such month…. he said such-and-such! You find the same in the practice of rhetoricians and men of letters when they gather the sayings of the wise: they arrange them by subject and idea, without recording when each was said. So it is with any sage: you find his sayings gathered into one book, just as Sahih al-Bukhari gathers the hadiths of the Messenger ﷺ, and we know for certain that he did not say them all in a single day!! Or the letters and essays of a thinker or philosopher: you find them collected in one volume, some of them undated. 2- Or they were all given on a single day. The timing of the messages There are always lessons you teach your child from time to time, and you are always asking yourself: what is the lesson I want to teach him? It is better to spread them over months and days than to pour them all out in one sitting, so that boredom, weariness and tedium, and then rejection, do not set in. That is why I lean strongly toward the first possibility. You see this in the way of the Prophet ﷺ: a counsel is a single line, a handful of words, unless the Companion says: “Tell me more.” And yes, some are several counsels given together. Then, in ordering the lessons by priority, he began 1- with creed and the oneness of Allah, 2- then with what grows his faith and his certainty that there is no bad deed and no good deed that Allah cannot bring forth, so as to bind his heart more closely to Allah. From this we understand that building certainty and good expectation of Allah is a basic, essential touchstone of upbringing, not a luxury! The prophets raised their children and their peoples on it (and if we marshalled all the evidence we would lose our subject! But it is plentiful: Noah, for instance, bidding his people seek forgiveness and promising that He would give them increase in wealth and children, and more besides..) This foundation is what shields children from psychological disorders, depression and anxiety, and keeps their faith from cracking and splitting apart. After laying solid roots for the boy's identity, he moved on to the branches: 3- establishing prayer, enjoining good and forbidding evil, patience, and spurring him toward resolve and lofty aims. So too a child must have his spirit roused and encouraged toward high things and great ambitions, toward rising above the petty and the trivial. High aspiration is something the young must be raised on. And once he had finished with the roots that form identity (creed and faith) and the branches of religion (prayer, enjoining good..) His son was ready to receive guidance on conduct and counsel on dealing with people, beginning with the warning against arrogance. Now notice with me (may Allah bless your hearing and your sight) that when he forbids ugly traits, he does not use the call of sonship! He does not say “O my son”! This is the height of refinement in teaching manners, the most beautiful of styles, the fullest tenderness and the soundest good omen. Had he said “O my son, do not be arrogant,” it would be as if he were saying that arrogance lived in his very self. But when you say: do not give arrogance any way into you, you set his self and his being apart from the ugly trait and put a great distance between them, so that he does not come near it, because you have kept “O my son” well away from it! And notice with me that he did not say to him: do not be arrogant! He did not use the plain word (arrogance); he used allusion! (And do not turn your cheek). He spoke of the cheek, the voice and the walk (your cheek, your pace, your voice) because they are real parts of the human self. He did not name arrogance itself, because it is not native to the soul, and so as not to plant it in him unawares, or plant stubbornness, by forbidding him in those words. And he closed with counsels of good taste and general manners (And be moderate in your pace…), which today go by the modern names of etiquette, taste and manners; it is well worth reading up on them and learning them! A puzzle! But why, when he forbade him from associating partners with Allah, did he say “O my son”?! The answer: because it was the opening of his counsel, so it had to begin with tenderness; and then because associating partners with Allah is a great injustice! It had to be rebuked and forbidden. It is fitting, then, in counsel on the roots and branches of religion, to use command, and in counsel on dealing with people, to use prohibition; and joining the two makes for the fullest understanding and grasp.

t: The Rule of the Human Mind According to Gustave Le Bon
x: For Gustave Le Bon, the rule of the human mind is to lead it from the composite to the abstract. For Gustave Le Bon, the rule of the human mind is to lead it from the composite to the abstract. And so, in his view, a child's upbringing must rest on what can be touched and seen, not on the abstract. My objection: this is simply not so! For a child, by his very nature, can grasp the most abstract of ideas, just as he believes in Allah by instinct. And even if he does not understand them now, hearing them again and again until he comes of age makes them easy for him to understand and to call to mind. Teach him the rules of grammar, and he may not understand them as a child; but at least the abstract notions will have passed before him: subject and object, declinable and indeclinable... Then, when he learns them again as a grown man, he grasps them clearly and easily, and imagines that age is what made the difference. True, in one sense; yet in another, it is the repetition, from childhood into adulthood, that made it. "O boy! I will teach you a statement: Be mindful of Allah and He will protect you. Be mindful of Allah and you will find Him before you. When you ask, ask Allah, and when you seek aid, seek Allah's aid..." Dr. Said al-Kamali commented on this hadith: "What would a child know of such vast meanings? We do not suppose that Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), as a boy, understood them. But this is no reason not to teach a child great ideas; he will understand them later, when he comes of age." What is more, if we built children's education on Le Bon's method, it would be a disaster! For, quietly and unseen, it raises the child on what is experimental and tangible alone, and a child raised this way will never be able to plant faith and values deep in his spirit and soul. The child must be taught what is abstract, but simply and gently, through similes and metaphors wherever we can.

t: Gustave Le Bon's Book (The Spirit of Education)
x: I read the book (The Spirit of Education) by the French thinker Gustave Le Bon I read the book (The Spirit of Education) by the French thinker Gustave Le Bon In it he takes on the problems of education in France and analyzes why European education had declined while American education excelled, in his day. It is an astonishing book, so let us talk through its most important points: Le Bon believes that the problems of education lie beneath the surface, out of sight; their causes are not the ones you would expect. The art of education is to turn the conscious into the unconscious. The Germans came to excel in education because they reformed it step by step, first changing public opinion and only then setting out the decisions, not rushing headlong. The answer is not to develop education by reforming the curricula or replacing the teachers, but to change the curricula and the programs together, wholly and comprehensively He criticizes an education that relies on the intellect alone, that works the memory and neglects every other thinking skill. He admires American education, where the teacher puts questions of explanation and observation to the student, and he notes that the laboratories in France stand empty, unused by teachers, while learning by discovery, experiment and hands-on work, using the senses, is essential. Le Bon opposes teaching dead languages that serve no purpose, and holds that living languages are enough. The rule of the human mind is to lead it from the compound to the abstract, and reforms in education should be built on the sciences of the nerves and the mind (and here I agree with him), for bad education comes from bad sources! So it makes no sense to give a child lessons in algebra and abstract concepts; you should start with what is tangible (here I don't quite agree! We will have a lively, delightful discussion about this point, if life allows) It is a waste of time to teach twenty ways of solving a problem when one or two are enough (I don't quite agree! Many methods widen the mind, showing it that there are broader paths to understanding and creativity) My critique: I agree with Le Bon in what I have set out above, but he seems to me heavily under the sway of the experimental method, so much so that even morals, for him, come from experience and practice, not from knowledge and books! Witty lines I enjoyed: “The assistant master is scorned by the professors, hated by the pupils and suspected by the headmaster; his life is hard beyond bearing.” Reforming education is like reforming religions: it took only a few messengers and a few books to reform the world. Professors who have learned doubt, cherished it and extended its reign over everything do not know that the evil, the whole evil, lies in teaching children to doubt. For nations are not built on doubt and suspicion but on faith and certainty, and no nation has a strong, productive existence unless it holds a strong, sincere faith in a lofty ideal it has taken as its aspiration”

t: Lemons and Yūsufī (“Mandarins”): On the Wisdoms in the Story of Yusuf
x: All through Surah Yusuf, one refrain: Knowing, Wise. All through Surah Yusuf, one refrain: Knowing, Wise. He knew, long before, with a perfect knowledge; and out of it He brought forth for Yusuf rulings and decrees that lead back to His knowledge, to the furthest end His judgment reached, the very point where His wisdom found its fulfillment. Among the wisdoms I have pondered in the story of Yusuf (peace be upon him): Allah willed to guide a number of the prisoners at his hands; had he not been there among them, they would never have known tawhid. Allah willed for Ya'qub (peace be upon him) a heart attached to the Truth rather than to creation; and He willed for Yusuf an exile and a solitude in which he would be cut off from creation and bound ever closer to the Truth. This is one of the purposes of solitude, of exile, of the departure of loved ones: to complete the blessing of tawhid upon the servant (and complete His favor upon you and upon the family of Jacob, as He completed it upon your fathers before, Abraham and Isaac. Indeed, your Lord is Knowing and Wise (6) Yusuf (This day I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favor upon you and have approved for you Islam as religion ۚ (3) (Al-Ma'idah). And once the blessing of tawhid is complete, He returns to the servant the beloved things he once knew, if He wills; for the wisdom has run its course, the good has been realized, and the blessing is complete. Prison, by its nature, is full of inmates quarreling among themselves; Allah dissolved those quarrels through tawhid and the call to Allah. It was also a training ground for Yusuf (peace be upon him) in untangling hard cases, for the day he would become the Aziz of Egypt and disputes would be brought before him. In the trial of chastity, a woman wishes for death, like Maryam (peace be upon her) (Oh, I wish I had died before this and was in oblivion, forgotten), while a man wishes for prison! (He said, "My Lord, prison is more to my liking than that to which they invite me." (33) Perhaps it is that a woman, by her very nature, is quicker to rush than a man, and her answer to a problem is to end it on the spot, while a man is steadier, slower and calmer. That is why the Lawgiver placed divorce in his hand and not in hers; had it been in hers, it would have been like death, something she longs for at every turn! (This does not hold for all men and all women.) Allah willed to show the despairing and the hopeless that He prevails over His affair, however the enemies scheme and whatever they do; when He wills a thing, He overpowers them. He cast him into the well to prepare him for a far longer stay in prison! So that he would know: just as He brought him out of the well before, with no might or power of his own, when he was small and weak, so He is able to bring him out of prison now that he is a grown and strong man. He gave him a way out of prison: the gift He had granted him of interpreting dreams. In the same way, the useful talents Allah blesses a person with may become his way out of whatever he is in, if he uses them well and benefits people through them. He asked nothing in return for interpreting the dream. And so it is with a person in the first days of climbing out of a crisis: small reward for the good his talent brings; then, afterward, the doors and the provisions swing open, as kingship came to Yusuf. Had he asked for money, he might well have angered the king; Yusuf (peace be upon him) knew better the king's temperament and his own position. But see how he put off the benefit, and the asking, until later ([Joseph] said, "Appoint me over the storehouses of the land."). So at the start of his path a person defers his gains, so they may grow great with time, and does not rush recklessly to claim them all at once and lose them all. Had Yusuf (peace be upon him) asked for a fee for the interpretation, he might have been given it, and then had nothing after it, no kingdom at all! But he deferred the gain and the taking, so that it would be greater with time. It was his patience through the trial of the prison, the well and his brothers' scheming that gave him this unhurried calm, the wisdom of moving step by step, and freedom from impulse and haste. Perhaps Yusuf's brothers had never tasted severe trial, and that is why they had so little wisdom. Whoever reads the characters of his brothers finds in them impulsiveness, haste and turmoil before the reconciliation came. Among this is their saying (Kill Joseph or cast him out to [another] land; the countenance of your father will [then] be only for you, and you will be after that a righteous people (9) (And they sold him for a reduced price - a few dirhams - and they were, concerning him, of those content with little (20) Had there been an atom of patience in them, they would have asked more money for him! But their only aim was to be rid of him, by any means, at even the paltriest price (So when they returned to their father, they said, "O our father, [further] measure has been denied to us, so send with us our brother [that] we will be given measure. And indeed, we will be his guardians" (63) The fā' signals immediate sequence (So when they returned): just like that! No easing into it, no gentle approach: send our brother Binyamin with us, come on! As though they had forgotten what they did to Yusuf, as though they had not yet regretted their deed! The criminal mind never knows regret. Their hasty nature shows, too, in what they said before the Aziz, with no regard for their brothers, no covering for them, no saving of face (They said, "If he steals - a brother of his has stolen before." ۚ(77) Had there been any modesty in them, any instinct to cover their own family, they would never have said such a thing before a stranger they did not know! Here, too, they cared for nothing but themselves: no concern for how their brothers and family looked to others, for their good name or anything else! Such concern is simply absent in those of base nature. Likewise, had they been at all deliberate, they would have asked what the ruling and law of the land were on taking a thief! ([The brothers] said, "Its recompense is that he in whose bag it is found - he [himself] will be its recompense." ۚ(75) They asked for no clarification, no time to consult; it seems their answer came all at once, in one voice. May Allah forgive them and pardon them. When an ignorant person will not answer to reason or good character, because emotion and desire have smothered him, it is better to withdraw, to leave, to flee; just as Yusuf admonished the wife of the Aziz, and when she would not stop, he fled from her. To carry on the conversation with people like these only opens the doors of evil, and there is no good in it. Praise be to Allah, and I seek forgiveness from Allah the Magnificent

t: The Most Merciful of the Merciful
x: (The Most Merciful of the merciful): throughout the Quran, this name is bound up with reconciliation between brothers and with drawing together those who have grown apart. (The Most Merciful of the merciful): throughout the Quran, this name is bound up with reconciliation between brothers and with drawing together those who have grown apart. So it helps to call upon this name when praying for reconciliation (O Most Merciful of the merciful, set things right between us) It is the supplication of Moses, peace be upon him ([Moses] said, "My Lord, forgive me and my brother and admit us into Your mercy, for You are the most merciful of the merciful." (151) And the supplication of Jacob, peace be upon him, for the quarrelling brothers (He said, "Should I entrust you with him except [under coercion] as I entrusted you with his brother before? But Allah is the best guardian, and He is the most merciful of the merciful." (64) And the supplication of Joseph for his brothers (He said, "No blame will there be upon you today. Allah will forgive you; and He is the most merciful of the merciful." (92) And the supplication of Job, peace be upon him, when people drew away from him And [mention] Job, when he called to his Lord, "Indeed, adversity has touched me, and you are the Most Merciful of the merciful." (83) So We responded to him and removed what afflicted him of adversity. And We gave him [back] his family and the like thereof with them as mercy from Us and a reminder for the worshippers [of Allah] (84) Disagreement is a mercy in jurisprudence and in culture; but when it descends upon societies and relationships, it becomes part of the punishment and the pain (Say, "He is the [one] Able to send upon you affliction from above you or from beneath your feet or to confuse you [so you become] sects and make you taste the violence of one another." Look how We diversify the signs that they might understand (65) These pains and torments needed a name that would pour mercy down upon them, so that they might become coolness and safety; and that name was (the Most Merciful of the merciful). He is more merciful to those at odds than they are to themselves. His mercy descends upon them and mends what is between them; the pain turns to coolness, and the rift to affection. His mercy means He is able to do this, even when minds had thought it impossible; and He forgives the slips and wrongs between them, so that they are better able to make peace (Perhaps Allah will put, between you and those to whom you have been enemies among them, affection. And Allah is competent, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful (7) The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: (Allah has an angel appointed over whoever says: O Most Merciful of the merciful. Whoever says it three times, the angel says: The Most Merciful of the merciful has turned toward you, so ask). (weak hadith) And there is no harm in using weak hadiths for the virtues of deeds

t: An Exposition of Surat al-Hadid for the One Seeking More
x: (Whatever is in the heavens and the earth exalts Allah, and He is the Almighty, the All-Wise (1) His is the dominion of the heavens and the earth; He gives life and causes death, and He has power over all things (2) He is the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden, and He has knowledge of all things (3) It is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days, then rose over the Throne.
