t: The Rope: One of the Names of the Quran
x: Fakhr al-Din al-Razi (may Allah have mercy on him) said that one of the names of the Quran is “ al-Ḥabl , the Rope: ﴿And hold firmly to the rope of Allah all together﴾ [Al Imran: 103]; in the exegesis, it is the Quran. It was given this name because whoever holds fast to it in the affairs of his religion is delivered by it from the punishment of the Hereafter and the chastisements of this world, just as one who clings to a rope is saved from drowning and from perils. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ called it a safeguard, saying: ‘This Quran is a safeguard for whoever holds fast to it,’ for it safeguards people from sins.” Fakhr al-Din al-Razi (may Allah have mercy on him) said that one of the names of the Quran is “ al-Ḥabl , the Rope: ﴿And hold firmly to the rope of Allah all together﴾ [Al Imran: 103]; in the exegesis, it is the Quran. It was given this name because whoever holds fast to it in the affairs of his religion is delivered by it from the punishment of the Hereafter and the chastisements of this world, just as one who clings to a rope is saved from drowning and from perils. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ called it a safeguard, saying: ‘This Quran is a safeguard for whoever holds fast to it,’ for it safeguards people from sins.” I say: a rope is for pulling, for pushing, for hauling up; it is used to rescue and to relieve. And the Quran pulls you toward Allah, hauls you along, even when a person has no wish for guidance and resists it. Merely holding on to one end of it (even a little reading, a little listening) keeps drawing him up and lifting him out of the depths of the well of sins, darkness, and ignorance, until little by little it raises him to the sky of nearness to Allah and of piety, of complete knowledge, of virtue and high standing, in this life and in the Hereafter. And this is borne out by the authentic hadith: “Indeed, I am leaving among you, that which if you hold fast to them, you shall not be misguided after me. One of them is greater than the other: The Book of Allah is a rope extended from the sky to the earth, and my family - the people of my house - and they shall not split until they meet at the Hawd, so look at how you deal with them after me” And this rope is the means through which one is given victory in this world and the Hereafter. The proof is the word of the Exalted: (Whoever should think that Allah will not support [him] in this world and the Hereafter - let him extend a rope ( sabab ) to the ceiling) Most exegetes hold that the sabab is a rope. And the rope is the Quran: whoever clings to it is given victory in this world and the Hereafter, and whoever cuts it, Allah leaves to go astray. And reflect on his words “so look at how you deal with them after me ( takhlufūnī )”: he used the language of succession, of leaving a trust to successors, while the Quran uses the language of inheritance and legacy: (Then we caused to inherit the Book those We have chosen of Our servants). It is the legacy of prophethood, left in our hands (how you deal with them after me). So look at where you stand with it! And mend it, mend it.

t: The Quran and Psychology: Which Does More to Change a Person’s Thought and Conduct?
c: Branches of the Relationship with the Quran
x: These are reflections and passing thoughts in which I set the Noble Quran’s way of changing a person beside psychology’s: in conduct, in belief, and in thought. These are reflections and passing thoughts in which I set the Noble Quran’s way of changing a person beside psychology’s: in conduct, in belief, and in thought. And where did they come from? From experience: some of it I witnessed, some I heard of, and some I lived myself on my journey of memorizing the Noble Quran, a journey of a year and nine months, by the grace of Allah the Exalted. I did not draw them from particular books or sources. I believe the truest knowledge is the knowledge that comes from the sweetness and the bitterness of experience. Books and studies can carry a surplus of philosophy that no one needs, like a tree so overgrown with branches and boughs, twigs and tendrils, that it begs to be pruned, and a person can barely find in it the fruit he came looking for. Lived experience, though, is the truer teacher, and brings the truth closer. And when I hold this up against psychology, I recall what Dr. Abdullah Al-Jaber said in an episode titled, I believe, “How Can We Be Happy in Our Relationships”: the trouble with psychology is that it has penned the human being into a very narrow space, the space of feelings and emotions. It has located all of a person’s ailments in the emotions alone: anxiety, depression, panic. Do you know of anything else? Has anyone ever told you there are other psychological ailments? Treatment and disorder alike are confined to feelings and emotions, as though a human being had no other troubles. Yet the human world of troubles is vast: troubles of the tongue, troubles of language, cultural troubles, social troubles, and much else besides, and troubles of the spirit and of faith. Dr. Abdullah Al-Jaber was right on these points when he said that the approach of Islam (or, to return to his own words, the approach of the Quran) is that a person’s ailments lie in the heart. In its way of changing people, the Noble Quran fixes its gaze on the diseases of the heart and sets them squarely before the eyes of whoever reads it and keeps its company. It speaks to us of the heart’s diseases, of doubt and hypocrisy, of vanity and showing off: (And [also] those who spend of their wealth to be seen by the people), and so much more. This does not mean psychology is wrong in everything. It has sound theories, and after Allah I owe it a debt: it helped me correct and change many ways of thinking and habits of mind, and more besides. I do not deny it; it is a respected discipline in its own right. But it has certain problems, and it is those certain problems we are speaking of. The Noble Quran works on moral healing, both in thought and in conduct. And seeking healing and treatment through the Noble Quran works differently from the psychological way: it rests on repetition, on a constant daily portion ( wird ) that a person never lets go of, and on deepening the relationship and letting it branch out: the “branches of the relationship with the Quran,” as I have named them. That is, a person will not draw healing and guidance from the Noble Quran unless he multiplies the branches of his bond with it. He must not settle for a portion of recitation alone, or for listening alone, but add to them understanding the Quran and its exegesis, reading about it, reflecting on it, and acting on it. And when a psychologist comes along and says, “Sometimes a man comes to me who has memorized the Noble Quran, an imam and preacher at a mosque, and still he has psychological problems!”, we call that psychologist to account and tell him: you should not say such things and spread them among people. Why? Because this is an individual problem, his problem alone; he may have misunderstood the Quran. Let us take an example: An educator, Dr. Mustafa Abu Saad, related in one of his episodes that a preacher and mosque imam came to his clinic with a psychological problem (no need to name it): a certain ugly addiction. So what was the cause? How can a man like that guard his prayers and still fall into such a thing? Stories like this unsettle the listener, who says to himself: so even religion won’t help, even the Quran won’t help, so why waste my time? That is why the case must be explained. He related that this man had used a legal stratagem ( ḥīlah fiqhiyyah ) to justify the wrong to himself. He said: “I know the Sharia, so I went searching until I found a fatwa that allowed me this thing, just as my desires and my mood wanted.” So the problem he fell into, the disease in his soul: he himself is its cause. Not the Quran, and not religion. The problem is his. Allah the Exalted says in Surat al-Baqarah: (In their hearts is disease). The scholars said this shows that the disease comes from the servant himself: (In their hearts); that is, the disease springs from the servant’s own soul, not from religion and not from the Quran, so do not lay it at the door of the Sharia. He has erred in his approach to the Quran, erred in his understanding of prayer, erred in his understanding of the Sharia. So why not explain this case to people? Why the sweeping statement? Why cite it and say, “I know many religious people, even a mosque preacher, who have addictions and problems”? Why not show us the error this man fell into, instead of tying things together in a way that clouds people’s understanding and plants doubt about their religion? I know this is not what the psychologist intends when he says it, but as long as it remains a sweeping statement, there is no call for it. This man erred in his way of understanding the Quran: he used a legal stratagem. Some scholars see no harm in using legal stratagems within their proper scope, to lift hardship and the like; but they are not to be used to slip free of what is forbidden, of the prescribed limits, and so on. So we come back to the question once more: when someone claims that the Noble Quran has not healed his problems and ailments, we say: that is because something is wrong in how he deals with the Quran and in his approach to it, and the problem may well be that he does not act on it. Allah the Exalted says in Surat al-Ma’idah: (Say, “O People of the Scripture, you are [standing] on nothing until you uphold [the law of] the Torah, the Gospel, and what has been revealed to you from your Lord.”), and that is the Quran. That is: you stand on nothing until you act on the Quran and live it out. It is not about memorizing the Quran so that when we ask you, “How many verses?” you have the answer ready ( mā shā’ Allāh ), or about memorizing it in all ten readings. There is something vital beyond that: that he upholds it. Allah the Exalted says: (And establish prayer). What does that mean? That he answers the call of prayer and keeps its conditions, its pillars, its obligations, its humility, and so on; that is, that he acts. If he does not act on the Quran, he is bound to run into problems; the ailments will linger in his soul, and the Quran will be of no benefit to him. Yes, for the Quran is either for you or against you. That is why one of the things that once held me back from memorizing the Quran was the poor examples I saw among those who had memorized it. Because they did not live by the Quran, I saw in them ugly, negative behavior and crooked character, and I would say: why should I memorize the Quran only to end up like them? To be frank, they set me a poor example. But my thinking changed after that, as I came to understand His words, the Exalted: (O you who have believed, upon you is [responsibility for] yourselves. Those who have gone astray will not harm you when you have been guided). That verse was my answer. If someone suffers from hypocrisy, or psychological ailments, or troubles of faith and spirit, that is because of him, not because of the Quran; he did not live it and did not act on it. Or the cause may be that he fell short in understanding the Quran. It is not as if a person simply reads the Quran and that is the end of it. You must keep a daily portion of the Quran, and that is a fine and beautiful thing; but for healing these problems and ailments, one must also be reminded to let the relationship branch out. To branch out the relationship means to bind yourself to the Quran in many ways: at times through understanding and exegesis, at times through reflection and contemplation, at times through listening and seeking healing. This is how seeking healing, and finding it, through the Noble Quran comes true. But to read without living it: then naturally he will fall into psychological troubles. And to read without understanding the Quran, without knowing what it says: then his healing through the Quran will be incomplete. Now we come to the Quran’s way of changing a person. It rests, as we said, on multiplying the branches of the relationship with the Quran, reflection and action among them, and on varying them, rather than keeping to only one kind of bond with the Quran. The second point: the Noble Quran brings about change through repetition. Memorizing the Quran depends on endless repetition; and after memorizing, the one who has memorized it keeps a set portion of the Quran, and that too is repetition. No sooner does he finish one portion, one complete reading, than he begins another; so the wisdom, the knowledge, and the healing wash over him again and again. This repetition plays its part in changing a person, and the power of repetition to change people is well known in media and in psychology. The third point: the way of long companionship, of sitting together and growing close. Whoever goes to a psychologist today sits with him for an hour or two, a session or two or three, and I doubt it is more than an hour or two, over a short, limited span. That is why a person may relapse (in psychology’s sense of the word): his bad habits come back, and he needs the clinic again. For the change psychology brings to the human soul is a change of the branches, not of the root; not fundamental, not essential, not radical. It changes the surface and leaves the depths untouched. That is why a person may spend perhaps eighteen years in psychology and its sciences, reading books and more, and nothing in him changes; in truth, his problems and his frustrations only grow. So tell me, then: why does the Quran turn a person a hundred and eighty degrees in a single year? Read about it, listen to the experiences and the stories of those who have memorized the Quran, and how the Quran changed them until they became someone other than who they had been; ([It will be] on the Day the earth will be replaced by another earth, and the heavens [as well]); and so too the human soul is replaced after the Quran: the soul is no longer the same soul, nor the spirit the same spirit. It is as if the Quran takes our old nervous system, throws it away, and hands us a new one. That is how I see it: it gives us new blood, a new spirit, a new life. So do not be surprised when you hear many who have memorized the Quran say: today I was born; today is my true birthday. And His words, the Exalted: (Say, “If Allah had willed, I would not have recited it to you, nor would He have made it known to you, for I had remained among you a lifetime before it. Then will you not reason?”). What I take from it (and this is my own reflection) is as if he were saying: my life and my years before the revelation came to me were one thing, and my life and my years after the revelation are something else entirely; after the Quran I was given a new birthday. (for I had remained among you a lifetime before it): I take from the verse that there is a lifetime after it, as though it were a new life. In any case, as we were saying: whoever goes to a psychologist sits with him for an hour, or two, or three, and so his change is no true change. But whoever memorizes the Noble Quran sits with the Quran five or six hours a day. Many who have memorized it say: we slept only four or five hours a day, and all the rest of the time we were reciting and repeating. And once he has memorized the Quran, he gives it his time so as not to forget it; otherwise, what was the point of the year or two he spent memorizing it? So the reciter and companion of the Quran, through long hours in its company, takes on the attributes and the names of the Quran. Among the names of the Quran: al-Karīm (the Noble), al-Ḥakīm (the Wise), and al-Muḥkam (the Firmly Set). And al-Muḥkam (the word just came to me), together with ḥukm (judgment) and ḥikmah (wisdom), all carry the sense that it holds a person in check: it governs his will, his desires, his whims, his thoughts, and his beliefs. For the Noble Quran disciplines a person in all these things: it is muḥkam , firmly set, and it makes a person firmly set. It is human nature for thoughts to come: let’s do this, and the Quran checks him, and he says: no, I don’t want to do that, I don’t want to say that. It makes a person firm, and the Quran shapes its reader with lofty qualities: the Quran is noble and makes its companion noble; the Quran is wise and makes its companion wise, so that you find in him marvelous reflections and beautiful insights into the Noble Quran. And the Quran is called al-ʿAẓīm , the Great, and its companion becomes great. In the sense of the authentic hadith, one of the Companions said: whoever among us had read al-Baqarah, that is, memorized it, rose high in our esteem; that is, he becomes a great person, and his greatness shows in how people take him to their hearts, and more. Another of the Quran’s names is the Rope: (And hold firmly to the rope of Allah), and the rope of Allah is the Quran. And in the sense of another authentic hadith: the Quran is the rope of Allah stretched from the sky to the earth, one end in the Hand of Allah, the other in the hand of the servant who holds fast to it. This image is always before my mind’s eye: I picture ropes let down from the sky to the earth, and those who have memorized the Quran clinging to them, while others hold no rope at all. I picture the whole globe, and people holding on to these ropes: these are the saved, by Allah’s leave, if Allah wills, for this lies in the Hand of Allah the Exalted. But these, the Quran saves from their cravings, saves from the adornment of this worldly life, its glitter, and its delusions. As Dr. Ahmed Abdel Moneim said: the more a person reads the Noble Quran, the more it loosens his hold on this world and kindles his longing for the Hereafter. And now I recall the verses of Surat al-Baqarah: (And who believe in what has been revealed to you, [O Muhammad], and what was revealed before you, and of the Hereafter they are certain [in faith]). Here restriction ( ḥaṣr ) is at work: certainty is confined to the Hereafter alone, as though certainty about anything else hardly counts. A person may be certain about this world, yet He confined certainty and reserved it for the Hereafter. Among the names of the Quran: the Light, and it passes its light on to its companion. And this light is a true, distinguishing light; that is, it wells up from the very core of the person. The hypocrite may benefit from the Quran too, but the benefit is slight and the light is slight, and whatever light the hypocrite has is an outer light, worn on the outside. The believer’s light, though, is an inner light, from within, because of the true and original light he carries in his heart. (Their example is that of one who kindled a fire, but when it illuminated what was around him, Allah took away their light): here Allah the Exalted describes the hypocrites as having light ( nūr ), and He did not say “their radiance” ( ḍiyāʾihim ), for the hypocrite has no radiance like the believer’s, only light (and light, as you know, is fainter and less than radiance). And (it illuminated what was around him) shows that the hypocrite’s light is an outer light, its source outside him. Further proof is the word istawqada , “kindled”: that is, he sought another’s help to kindle this fire. Had this light come from his own essence and core, He would have said awqada , “lit”; but He said istawqada . So the believer’s light is original and true: the Quran lights up his face, his heart, his spirit, and his tongue. And here too the limits of psychology as a means of change come into view: it changes only feelings and the lightest of things. The Noble Quran’s change, however, reaches everything: it changes even the tongue, even the language; even a person’s eloquence is transformed, even his memory. You hear those who memorize the Quran say: our memory has grown strong. And do not even ask about this, for those who have memorized the Quran do not speak of it; they live, truly, in bliss, but some of them keep that bliss to themselves, guarding it, afraid for it. And I say: every pleasure short of the Quran is incomplete. When a person memorizes the Quran, reflects on it, and truly reaches it, his pleasure is complete, even if the pleasures around him fall short, even if the world around him falls short. Sheikh Abdulsalam Al-Shuwaier related in one of his lectures that a non-Arab Muslim had memorized the Quran and never slipped in its grammar; the Sheikh said: I did not find a single mistake in him. Why? Because the Noble Quran had passed its eloquence on to him. Among the Quran’s names are al-Bayān (the Clear Statement) and al-Mubīn (the Clear): (These are the verses of the clear Book); and so it passes on to its companion clarity, eloquence, and language, and it straightens and heals a person’s troubles of tongue and speech. Does psychology do this? Psychology treats a limited range of things. And we do not belittle the worth of psychology; these are reflections, not idle talk. It is a discipline in its own right that people study for years, and no one should come along and stamp it “wrong”! Nor do we downplay its importance; it matters, and its theories matter. But we are pointing out certain problems in it: it confines the human being to the psyche alone, then confines the psyche to emotions and feelings, while the human being, as a whole and in every part, is far greater than that. A person has a bond with his Lord, and in that bond there are problems he must resolve, and the Quran helps him resolve them. He has troubles in his bond and his dialogue with himself, and troubles in his bond with others and his dealings with them; and the Noble Quran heals all of these. And then there is the question of the source, as Dr. Ahmed Abdel Moneim observed (and we salute him for it): the schools of psychology, Freud’s psychoanalysis, then behaviorism, and others, have their problems and their errors, because they are made by human beings. But Allah, glorified and exalted is He, is the One who created human beings and the human soul, and He knows best what sets it right and what flaws it holds: (Does He who created not know, while He is the Subtle, the Acquainted?). Allah the Exalted knows this soul best, and what sets it right, and what heals it; and that is why the Noble Quran is the soundest and finest of all ways to straighten and reshape the human soul.

t: Reflecting on the Words of the Exalted {They said, “O our father, why do you not entrust us with Joseph”}
x: Then, after they had betrayed him and came asking for his second brother, Benjamin, (He said, “Should I entrust you with him except [under coercion] as I entrusted you with his brother before?”)? Then, after they had betrayed him and came asking for his second brother, Benjamin, (He said, “Should I entrust you with him except [under coercion] as I entrusted you with his brother before?”)? Notice the word the two verses share: taʾmannā , “entrust us,” and āmanukum , “entrust you”? A person gives his trust and his sense of safety once; wound him, and he will doubt a thousand times, and neither trust nor feel safe again It was Jacob's shrewdness, peace be upon him, that when they pressed him to let Benjamin go, he bound them with oaths and pledges and made an exception (He said, “Never will I send him with you until you give me a promise by Allah that you will bring him [back] to me, unless you should be surrounded by enemies”). Here is a lesson: the one who has been betrayed is entitled not to trust the betrayer, even if he betrayed only once. And if he does extend his trust, let it be with caution and care, guarded and watchful, by taking pledges, writing things down, contracts, witnesses and other such means, so that his right is secure and kept safe This is the nature of the human mind: it builds on its first judgment, its first experience. That is why, when they told him that the Aziz had taken Benjamin, though this time they were telling the truth, (He said, “Rather, your souls have enticed you to something”). He said it because he was human, and the natural judgments of human beings ran their course in him too. Otherwise, Allah's prophet Jacob, peace be upon him, was praised by Allah for his knowledge (And indeed, he was a possessor of knowledge because of what We had taught him), so nothing he said takes away from his knowledge. And for all the pain of those two bitter experiences (losing Joseph, then Benjamin), his good expectation of Allah stood very high. This, and Allah knows best, is the knowledge for which he was praised, and the fruit that knowledge bears: reverent awe and good expectation of Allah (He said, “Rather, your souls have enticed you to something, so patience is most fitting. Perhaps Allah will bring them to me all together. Indeed it is He who is the Knowing, the Wise”), and his words (O my sons, go and find out about Joseph and his brother and despair not of relief from Allah. Indeed, no one despairs of relief from Allah except the disbelieving people). What we learn from this is that a person should not judge by his first experience just because it failed and disappointed him; the second may bring success and great reward. Building on that first experience (which brings back the frustration, the resentment, the despair and the rest) robs him of chances to understand, to build relationships, to produce and to work. So many good things have slipped away from us only because we built on the bitterness of the first time Nor should a person judge all of creation, all people, through one lens and one picture; that comes from a narrow soul and from ignorance. Rather, let his judgments of them vary, sometimes thinking well of them, sometimes ill Dr. Wahbah al-Zuhayli said, on the qualities of a judge: “Knowing people and their conditions, and seeing through their cunning and deceit. He should not think well of them; rather, he should be wary and alert to what they dress up in their questions, lest they become skilled at what is wrong. The hadith adds to this: «Guard yourselves against people by thinking ill of them».” And among these qualities: that he should study tales of plots, tricks and cunning, and sit with his enemies and his friends alike to gain this knowledge! For it is not found in books but in gatherings. So that he is not taken in, but stays alert and sharp. For whoever falls for a deception falls because he did not know it; and every trick that failed to fool you failed, first, because Allah granted you success, and second, because you knew it for what it was

t: Rich Through the Quran
x: {And He found you lost and guided [you], and He found you poor and made [you] self-sufficient} {And He found you lost and guided [you], and He found you poor and made [you] self-sufficient} The exegetes differed over how Allah found His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ poor and made him self-sufficient, when the Messenger of Allah never had such wealth, such riches, such money? They said it is explained by the authentic hadith of the Messenger of Allah: “Richness does not lie in the abundance of goods (wealth and possessions), but richness is the richness of the soul” I say: this verse {And He found you poor and made [you] self-sufficient} is bound to the one before it {And He found you lost and guided [you]}. He found you lost and guided you by revelation, by the Quran; and He found you poor in soul, weak in soul, scattered and torn apart, sorrowful and desolate, frightened and burdened with care; so He made your soul rich with the Quran and fed the hunger of your spirit with revelation. Then your scattered self was gathered, your spirit found its companion, your heart grew tranquil, and your trembling heart was stilled. Keep a daily portion of the Quran and never part from it; you will reach the richness of the spirit, its scattered pieces will be gathered, your spirit will find its rest, and your soul will grow ever steadier and firmer before hardships and calamities. Among his supplications ﷺ was “O Allah, revive me,” that is: revive my heart and make it strong. And what revives the heart and makes it strong, if not the Quran? And it is related in a saying: "The Quran: no poverty after it, and no richness without it" His words ﷺ “He is not one of us who does not yataghanna with the Quran” bear two meanings: being enriched by it, needing nothing beyond it ( istighnāʾ ); and the other meaning: the beautiful voice. So the meaning may be: he is not one of us who does not find his richness in the Quran and is not content with it {And is it not sufficient for them that We revealed to you the Book which is recited to them?} And in the explanation of the words of the Exalted {[Allah] said, "O Moses, I have chosen you over the people with My messages and My words [to you]. So take what I have given you and be among the grateful"}, that is: take it, let it suffice you, and do not stretch your eyes toward anything else. And this is His saying, Exalted is He: {And We have certainly given you, [O Muhammad], seven of the often repeated [verses] and the great Qur'an. Do not extend your eyes toward that by which We have given enjoyment to [certain] categories of the disbelievers, and do not grieve over them. And lower your wing to the believers}. Abu Talib al-Makki relates in Qut al-Qulub : "One of the shaykhs told me, concerning its meaning, that one of the reciters who were close to Allah was struck by such dire poverty that it grieved him and he was at his wits' end. He said: Then he saw in a dream someone saying to him: Would you like Us to make you forget Surat al-An'am, and have a thousand dinars instead? He said: No. Then Surat Hud? He said: No. Then Surat Yusuf? He said: No. He said: Then you carry with you the worth of a hundred thousand, and you complain of poverty! And he woke with his sorrow lifted from him. And so it came in the report: ( Taghannaw with the Quran, that is, be enriched by it; whoever is not enriched by the verses of Allah the Exalted, may Allah, Mighty and Majestic, never enrich him. The Quran is the richness with which there is no poverty and beyond which there is no richness; and whoever is given the Quran by Allah and then thinks that anyone is richer than he has mocked the verses of Allah the Exalted. And in another wording: has made light of what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent down). And in the well-known hadith: ((Whoever does not yataghanna with the Quran is not one of us)). And in the concise report: ((Certainty is enough of a richness)); and the Quran is the very truth of certainty."

t: Reflecting on the Saying of the Exalted (Or [it is] like a rainstorm from the sky)
x: Allah likened the Quran to the ṣayyib , the rain. Exegesis Allah likened the Quran to the ṣayyib , the rain. Reflection That He said ka-ṣayyib ("like a rainstorm") and not ka-maṭar ("like rain"); because the mark of the ṣayyib is lasting benefit, unlike maṭar , which may come as relief and may come as punishment And Abu Ubaydah said: when it is punishment, it is " amṭarat ," and when it is mercy, it is " maṭarat ." And this is why the Messenger of Allah said in the supplication: We have had a rainfall ( muṭirnā ) due to the Blessing and Mercy of Allah. Muṭirnā is derived from maṭar And His saying, the Exalted, {if you are troubled by rain}: what is meant here is certainly al-ghayth , relief-giving rain. And Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) used the word maṭar : Narrated Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her): ((Whenever Allah's Messenger ﷺ saw the rain, he used to say, "O Allah! Let it be a strong fruitful rain ( ṣayyiban nāfiʿan )" )) That the mark of the ṣayyib is benefit, and the Quran is of immense benefit to its companion, a safety for him that brings him no harm "because whoever holds fast to the Quran is safe from harm in this world and the Hereafter " — Fakhr al-Din al-Razi And the companion of the Quran takes on this quality: he is a source of good to all creation and brings harm to no one. Rain may be scant and may be plenty, but the ṣayyib is abundant, heavy and dense; and so is the Quran for the believer: rich in benefit, its blessings in this world and the Hereafter beyond counting. That the Quran is a ṣayyib that puts out the fires of trials, calamities and turmoil; and the accounts of those people of old are full of this: one who recited his daily portion of the Quran, and through it Allah put out a trial or a calamity and turned it away from him. He sees it with his own eyes and hears it with his own ears. And the ṣayyib brings many kinds of good: it benefits livestock, creatures, people, the land, the mountains and the fruits; and the Quran — every letter of it brings its companion ten good deeds —and Allah multiplies for whom He wills— and light, knowledge and wisdom. And its companion brings many kinds of good That the soul, after the ṣayyib has come down, feels rest, joy and gladness — and that is just what the reciter of the Quran feels when he finishes his daily portion

t: Reflections on the Words of Allah the Exalted (even if their plan had been [sufficient] to do away with the mountains)
x: Whoever is targeted by plots, schemes and injustice, this itself points to his greatness, for Allah measured it against the mountain, the mightiest of His creations; and it is proof of the greatness of Muhammad ﷺ. Whoever is targeted by plots, schemes and injustice, this itself points to his greatness, for Allah measured it against the mountain, the mightiest of His creations; and it is proof of the greatness of Muhammad ﷺ. Whoever is targeted by plotting: the mountains give way, but he does not, so complete is Allah's protection of him, so perfect His care, so all-encompassing His knowledge of him And it is proof that he stands firmly rooted in the land, however the heavens and the earth may scheme against him. For the mountains are firmly rooted in the land, yet they would give way if such plotting were aimed at them; while the righteous believer, once rooted in the land, stands firm as the mountains, and his mark is never wiped out or worn away (They want to extinguish the light of Allah with their mouths, but Allah refuses except to perfect His light, although the disbelievers dislike it) Here is proof that Muhammad ﷺ is greater than the mountains in steadfastness and uprightness, more firmly rooted, longer in reach and in character (And indeed, you are of a great moral character).

t: The Final Episode of Life: Reunion After Parting
x: And hearts grew calm, and souls came to rest; sparrows singing out and nightingales trilling, “and the splendid sun, the sun has risen, and the world is a wedding feast.” The sky! Even the sky dressed itself in the colors of the rainbow and wore the hours of the full moon, and the clouds turned and fled And hearts grew calm, and souls came to rest; sparrows singing out and nightingales trilling, “and the splendid sun, the sun has risen, and the world is a wedding feast.” The sky! Even the sky dressed itself in the colors of the rainbow and wore the hours of the full moon, and the clouds turned and fled Look: Yusuf meets his father; he goes out to receive the caravan. Before that he was reunited with his brothers, and before that with his brother. A bitter parting, a family torn apart, every line of contact cut: that is the first episode of life. They threw him into the depths of the well; then came bitter episodes and tearful nights (And they came to their father at night, weeping). The soul grew weary and gave out, the days and nights turned their backs and fled, the caravans headed home. What is left to wait for! Wait! The episode isn't over yet, Then, little by little, the family is gathered back together. He is reunited with his brother Benjamin (he took his brother to himself; he said, “Indeed, I am your brother, so do not despair over what they used to do [to me]”). And this was a signal to Yusuf: if he could be reunited with one close to him, then his greatest love, his father, he would meet too, but only in the final minutes, when the blessing is complete and old age has devoured the morsel. Then he is reunited with his brothers: (He said, “No blame will there be upon you. Today Allah will forgive you; and He is the most merciful of the merciful”), following the recitation of Warsh from Nafi', where the pause falls at ʿalaykum , “upon you.” So the meaning becomes: the day they are reunited is the day of pardon, of generosity, of sins forgiven. Then he meets his greatest love: his father (he took his parents to himself) A small homecoming heralds the greater Eid al-Adha (And when they entered upon Joseph, he took his brother to himself; he said, “Indeed, I am your brother, so do not despair over what they used to do [to me]”) (And when they entered upon Joseph, he took his parents to himself and said, “Enter Egypt, Allah willing, safe [and secure]”) [Scene Two: Silent, No Script] She casts him into the river, a nursing infant.. Which will he meet first? The darkness of the pitch-black night, or the darkness of the deadly sea, or the cruelty of a fate that carried him far from his mother's tender breast? On the shore of safety, he meets his enemy. Safety and tenderness, both gone. She wept; her heart cracked and trembled in terror at losing him (And the heart of Moses' mother became empty [of all else]. She was about to disclose [the matter concerning] him had We not bound fast her heart that she would be of the believers) There is a good promise here, the kind that promises reunion after parting, a true promise, beyond all doubt And like Yusuf, the infant was first reunited with his sister (And she said to his sister, “Follow him”), as if to say: just as I could bring you someone close to you (when your sister went and said, “Shall I direct you to someone who will be responsible for him?”), so I am able to bring you the dearest heart of all, the closest and nearest to you (So We restored him to his mother that she might be content and not grieve and that she would know that the promise of Allah is true. But most of the people do not know). The very words of the mother are the words of the father! (And when the bearer of good tidings arrived, he cast it over his face, and he returned [once again] seeing. He said, “Did I not tell you that I know from Allah that which you do not know?”) What did the old man Yaqub, peace be upon him, know? And what did the mother know? They knew that Allah's promise of reunion is true, even if it comes only in the Gardens, when lifespans and hopes have run out; true, beyond all doubt (Indeed, you are to die, and indeed, they are to die. Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, will dispute) It may be a reckoning over wrongs, or the reproaches of loved ones. [Scene Three / The Hardest Plot] He falls ill until he is at death's door And all his loved ones and children are parted from him, Which will he meet first: the illness that has imprisoned his body, or the loss of his own flesh and blood! He suffers until it towers over him ( samāhu ) and he gives it a name ( sammāhu ): (adversity) (And [mention] Job, when he called to his Lord, “Indeed, adversity has touched me”) And it was adversity because everyone had strayed away from him, and he was left alone with his first Beloved: my Lord and his Lord, Allah (And when adversity touches you, lost are [all] those you invoke except for Him) Then help came, and reunion, and a whole army of family (So We responded to him and removed what afflicted him of adversity. And We gave him [back] his family and the like thereof with them as mercy from Us and a reminder for the worshippers [of Allah]) (And We granted him his family and a like [number] as mercy from Us and a reminder for those of understanding) A reminder for the people of reason! And a reminder for the worshippers! That where parting ends, reunion begins. This is Allah's way in His creation; but you are hasty. (The Parting of the Angry One) He left his people in anger at them; so he lost land and sea and earth and sank into darkness upon darkness, until his people thought he would never return, And he returned The same story as Ayyub's, illness and parting (But We threw him onto the open shore while he was ill); only here it is parting, then illness! The order doesn't matter, for all of us pass through these decrees.. but knowledge and wisdom depend on which of them came first. What matters is this: tell me, whom do you resemble, Dhun-Nun or Ayyub? Then came healing and reunion (And We caused to grow over him a gourd vine. And We sent him to [his people of] a hundred thousand or more). And when the reunion came, it was finer than the parting For they were better in faith and character than he had left them Had that parting never happened, faith would have made no difference to them Perhaps a parting brought about repentance; perhaps a separation brought knowledge to light. (Two Partings, or Three, Maybe More / Viewer Warning: Not for the Faint of Heart) The hardest parting is to be driven away by the one you love, And for the One you love to command you to part from the one you love, His father drove him out ([His father] said, “Have you no desire for my gods, O Abraham? If you do not desist, I will surely stone you, so avoid me a prolonged time”) He left his house, his homeland, his land Then Allah commands him to kill his son with his own hand! A parting that comes about without your hand And a parting that comes about by your hand Both are bound to come in life (Indeed, this was the clear trial) The parting that comes without your hand is decree And the parting that comes by your hand is choice: to choose the righteous and part from the wicked. Not because you are perfect, of course! But a person can barely hold on to his own goodness, so we have no time to argue over a road we have already chosen. (The Parting of the Coerced and the Reunion of the Compelled / A Sad Scene) (and made its people into factions) Pharaoh cut the Children of Israel apart and tore them into groups so that they could not come together, by coercion and force, and so that dominion and sovereignty would never be theirs. And in the verse there is iḥtibāk ! That is, leaving out the end because the beginning points to it: the end of the story, their reunion, is left out, and its beginning, their scattering, is mentioned (and made its people into factions). Meaning: what looks like parting on the outside is, on the inside, the mercy of reunion (So We restored him to his mother that she might be content and not grieve) (A Scene That May Be Merged with the Previous One) Enmities, grudges, anger, hatred, a face that cannot bear the sight of another face. Whoever has insight can see how it ends: (Perhaps Allah will put, between you and those to whom you have been enemies among them, affection. And Allah is competent, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful) Every “perhaps” ( ʿasā ) in the Quran is binding: certain to happen and to come true. Let the mind or the soul deny it; it is coming, it is surely coming, because it is recompense (And indeed, the recompense is to occur). Competent to mend what was severed And Forgiving and Merciful: He forgives what lies between those at odds, turns to them so that they may turn back to Him, then makes peace between them; (and settlement is best), and is there any good that is not from Allah? (O Prophet, when you [Muslims] divorce women…) until He said (You know not; perhaps Allah will bring about after that a [different] matter) You do not know the unseen, O veiled one, nor the decrees it holds, nor what is hidden from eyes behind its curtains. Perhaps a return after a divorce; perhaps a reunion after a parting. For the whole matter belongs to Allah.

t: Islam and the System of Rewards and Motivation
x: Islam has a wonderful system of rewards, motivation, encouragement and hope; part of it is the feast, the sharing of food, however little, at every joy that comes to completion or begins. Among these: the wedding feast ( walīmat al-ʿurs , a firmly established Sunnah); the ʿaqīqah at a birth, boy or girl (Sunnah); the shundukhiyyah , at the betrothal and the marriage contract (the beginning of a marriage); the wakīrah , food for a newly built home; the naqīʿah , food for the return of one who was away; and the mishdākh , when a reciter completes the Quran. Islam has a wonderful system of rewards, motivation, encouragement and hope; part of it is the feast, the sharing of food, however little, at every joy that comes to completion or begins. Among these: the wedding feast ( walīmat al-ʿurs , a firmly established Sunnah); the ʿaqīqah at a birth, boy or girl (Sunnah); the shundukhiyyah , at the betrothal and the marriage contract (the beginning of a marriage); the wakīrah , food for a newly built home; the naqīʿah , food for the return of one who was away; and the mishdākh , when a reciter completes the Quran. A feast for funerals and condolences, however, is disliked, except for food made for the family of the deceased alone, so that feasting never becomes bound up with grief. And so, when we look at what Islam legislates about feasts, we find them bound up with joy. And at every stage where a person moves on and changes for the better Food is shared, even a little; let it be intended as charity and as thanks to Allah, for thanks draws down more, and as joy in Allah's bounty and blessing. {Say, "In the bounty of Allah and in His mercy - in that let them rejoice"} that one should rejoice that the blessing came from Allah, not from oneself. So do not keep the reward for yourself; make it charity, joy and thanks to Allah, and it will mean so much more. For “Once the Prophet ﷺ distributed dates among his companions and gave each one seven dates” (narrated by al-Bukhari). Nor do I agree with those who say: “Graduation parties, and feasts for studies, for a new job, for a betrothal or a new home, are innovations, novelties alien to our society!” Anyone who reads the Shari'ah of Islam deeply knows that it encourages such things, for they fall under charity, feeding others and gratitude. And I can only see the one who says this (that they are new and an innovation) as either stingy, or blind to the occasions for charity and for feeding others, a stranger to the occasions for gratitude, or else a gloomy soul who has never valued a blessing as it deserves. So when someone becomes skilled at something and masters it, let him give something in charity, however small: Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal handed out walnuts to the boys, five apiece, when his son al-Hasan mastered his lessons. And on completing a stage of learning (even if other stages remain): as Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) and his son did when they slaughtered a camel upon learning Surat al-Baqarah. And whoever has memorized 114 surahs may, without any blame, hold 114 celebrations! And so it is with every other craft, science and art.

t: An Epistle on the Limits of Thoughts / 1
x: Know (may Allah grant us and you success) that hearts have their earnings, and minds have their limit. Know (may Allah grant us and you success) that hearts have their earnings, and minds have their limit. The earnings of the heart are its deeds: the passing thoughts it lets settle within it, the delights and the tears it has laid up in store. And this is His saying (but He imposes blame upon you for what your hearts have earned). And minds have a limit where they must end and halt; were they to cross it, they would destroy crops and animals, (And Allah does not like corruption), not even in the mind does He like it! For the mind is the field where thoughts are sown, the seedbed of deeds, the nursery of the soul, the food of subtle graces, the drawing-near of secrets, the storehouse of tidings. Inspiration from the Lord, the Exalted, is an honour and a mark of His generosity, and it is fitting that it descend only upon pure ground: just as one who remembers Allah ought not to eat garlic and onion, and one who prays may not pray in a place of impurity. Those who know Allah know that whoever is deprived of subtle graces and insights, whose heart is veiled from them, owes it to a sin his heart and mind have earned, not his limbs. Do you not know that the recompense matches the deed? For these subtle graces are hidden knowledge, veiled from creation and reserved for the servant; their rapture ( wajd ) steals into his inner being, and so he finds them ( wajadahā ). Fakhr al-Din al-Razi (may Allah have mercy on him) said of the words of the Exalted (In their hearts is disease, so Allah has increased their disease): it is the withholding of any further graces. So what the heart earns either veils understanding, or polishes the inner sight until it understands from the All-Knowing. This, then, is the sorrow of those who know: states they once harvested, subtle graces they once beheld, then veiled from them by the sins of the heart. This is their sorrow in this world, and nothing besides. The Sufis went too far, carried to excess in annihilation and eternity, in ceaseless contemplation in the presence of the Eternal Refuge. For a human being, whoever he may be, needs to reflect on his life in this world just as on his life in the next Have you not heard His words: (that you might give thought to this world and the Hereafter)? By this He means reflection on the interests and affairs of this world and on its sciences, on how things work and how they are to be managed; for no deed is sound unless the thought behind it is sound. Now that you know this (may Allah keep you safe), let us move on to its limits The Limits of Reflecting on This World Whatever is outwardly permissible is inwardly permissible too, that is, it is permissible to think about; and whatever is outwardly forbidden to the limbs, it is forbidden even to think about! Between the two lie doubtful matters, and according to the light of those who know and their degrees of piety, understanding shines forth and scrupulousness grows strong. Know this, and you will be safe. (And know that Allah knows what is within yourselves, so beware of Him) "He warned them about what passes through their hearts concerning women, and guided them to harbour good rather than evil; then He did not leave them despairing of His mercy, nor hopeless of His kindness, but said: (And know that Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing)" - Ibn Kathir This verse comes in the context of proposing marriage; and since most passions fall within that domain, it is cited here. It is fitting, then, for the resolute and the shrewd to pack away the baggage of his passions and emotions and cut them off, and for the brave and the noble to stand against the current of his nature and master it; for this is the great summit, the great resolve, the farthest reach. We have said: even if he feels love, no one is held to account for a feeling, so long as he does not drink from the cup of imaginings, nor let himself drift into what feeds them. And the one truly strong and trustworthy, firm of heart, is he who stands guard at the frontiers of imaginings and memories, strips himself of them, and says: "Allah, Allah is my Lord, I do not associate anything as partner with Him." (And take your provision from the skills psychology offers for mastering your thoughts, for they are truly useful; take them in search of purity from passions, and for the journey to the Lord of the worlds) The Limits of Reflecting on the Hereafter One reflects on it in submission, humility and awe, not in the manner of those who plunge into the knowledge of the unseen and philosophize about the Lord's attributes (exalted is He, high above what they say). Rather, let him reflect on Paradise until his soul yearns for it, and picture himself standing before the Lord of the worlds and being questioned; and let him strive to summon fear, humility and love, for the seeker begins by striving and ends by arriving, rightly guided. And when he slips into thoughts of passion, let him not excuse himself with pleas of weakness and escape. For Yusuf (peace be upon him) had ten excuses counted for him to fall into sin, and still he did not! He was young, a stranger, unmarried; and she was the queen of the palace, from whom commands and prohibitions flowed. Yet for all that he fled from her and refused her, and so he humbled her, and was himself raised in honour. So put your excuses aside; even the prophets lived in times of trial, and you are not the only one being tested.

t: Bend, O Streams
x: Bend, O streams Bend, O streams And draw upon the earth a straight line, For bending teaches the mountains to stand upright. Bend, O streams, Spread your water along the paths of light; Shine for the lion and the dervish, Glimmer for the sultan and the donkeys. Everyone drinks from you, For all are thirsty. Bend, O streams; Around you the nightingales warble, The birds sing, and the sun soars across the horizons. And say to the sun: Set, or do not set, O daughter of the yellow one, for I will stand in your place, giving light through the long nights. We are the embrace of the hunted and the outcast, of the seeker of truth, the one gone astray in the village, accused of shedding blood. Let him drink from you, let him slake his thirst at the suns of your light; spread uprightness out before him, and welcome him in the night, So that if he steals, you pour the awe of majesty over his imagination, and he turns back to the paths of uprightness.
